docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The CO.STARTERS Canvas Framework
  • Chapter 4: Customer Discovery & Segmentation

docs.title: The Second Block: What Are They Actually Struggling With?
docs.text:
Chapter 4 gave you a sharp, specific customer. This chapter answers the question that customer's existence only raises: what, precisely, are they struggling with? A vague answer here — "grooming is inconvenient," "dinner is stressful" — produces a Solution block that's just as vague. This chapter's job is turning a fuzzy sense that "this bothers people" into a Problem block sharp enough to test.

Getting Specific About Pain

"People are busy" is not a problem statement — it's an observation about the entire human species. By the end of this chapter, you'll know how to turn that kind of vague observation into a problem sharp enough to test against real people. Let's find out for real!

docs.title: What Counts as a Real Problem
docs.text:
Problem definition is the practice of stating, in specific and falsifiable terms, the difficulty your target customer experiences that your venture intends to address — specific enough that someone could look at real evidence and say whether the statement is true or false for that customer. This is the second block on the canvas, and it inherits everything Chapter 4 established: a problem is only ever a problem for a specific target customer, not for people in general.

Two smaller terms build up to that definition. Customer pain is the negative experience — frustration, cost, wasted time, embarrassment, risk — a customer feels as a direct result of an unsolved problem. A pain point is one specific, nameable instance of that pain, concrete enough to describe in a single sentence: not "grooming is a hassle" but "I have to take an unpaid afternoon off work to drive forty minutes each way." Jordan's problem definition, refined after several Field Discovery Windows, reads: "Dog owners within 5 miles who don't own a car-friendly crate lose a half-day of income or personal time every time their dog needs grooming, because the nearest groomer requires an in-person drop-off and pickup." That's specific enough to test — and specific enough to be wrong, which is exactly what makes it useful.

docs.title: Real Problems vs Perceived Problems
docs.text:
Not every problem a founder believes in turns out to be real. A real problem is one that customers actually experience and can describe from their own lived frustration when asked directly, confirmed through evidence rather than founder intuition. A perceived problem is one a founder believes customers have, based on logic, outside research, or their own experience, that has not yet been confirmed by talking to the actual target customer. Every problem starts as perceived — the only way a perceived problem becomes a real one is problem validation: the process of testing a perceived problem against real customer conversations and behavior to confirm whether it is genuinely felt, exactly as urgently as assumed.

A Perceived Problem Isn't a Mistake — It's a Starting Point

Notice that "perceived" doesn't mean "wrong." Every real problem this course has ever validated started out perceived. The only mistake is treating a perceived problem as if it were already real — building a Solution block around it before a single customer has confirmed it from their own mouth.

docs.title: Finding the Root Cause
docs.text:
Even a confirmed, real problem can be stated at the wrong depth. A symptom is the surface-level complaint a customer voices first, while a root cause is the underlying condition actually producing that complaint — often several layers beneath the first thing anyone says out loud. Symptom vs. root cause is the discipline of not stopping at the first explanation a customer offers, because a solution built for a symptom often leaves the root cause untouched.

Priya ran into this directly. Her interviewees' first complaint was almost always "I don't have time to cook." That's a symptom. Asking "why don't you have time" repeatedly — a technique sometimes called the Five Whys — led somewhere more specific: not a lack of hours in the day generally, but the unpredictability of rotating shift schedules making any planned dinner routine fall apart. The root cause wasn't time scarcity; it was schedule unpredictability. A meal kit requiring advance planning would have solved the symptom's surface complaint while missing the root cause entirely.

Two more ideas sharpen this same search. An unmet need is a customer requirement that no current option — including doing nothing — adequately satisfies, whether or not the customer has ever put it into words. A job to be done reframes the whole question around function rather than feature: the underlying task or outcome a customer is fundamentally trying to accomplish, independent of any particular product, such as "get a nutritious dinner on the table with zero advance planning" rather than "buy a meal kit."

Before trying the interactive drill-down, notice that the technique is always the same: take the first complaint, ask "why" again, and keep going until the answer stops changing.

docs.title: Diagram: Symptom vs Root Cause Drill-Down
docs.text:
Symptom vs Root Cause Drill-Down

Type: microsim sim-id: symptom-root-cause-drilldown Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: apply

Learning objective: Given a customer's first-stated complaint, learners apply a repeated "why" technique, choosing at each step which underlying cause to pursue, to trace the symptom down to its root cause.

Canvas layout:

  • Top: the current complaint text in a card
  • Below: 2-3 candidate "why" answers presented as clickable buttons
  • A running vertical trail on the left showing each previously selected layer, top (symptom) to bottom (current depth)

Behavior: Start with Priya's complaint: "I don't have time to cook." Present 2 candidate answers to "Why not?": (a) "There aren't enough hours in the day" (a dead-end distractor that loops back to the same complaint if chosen — with feedback: "This restates the symptom rather than explaining it — try the other option"), (b) "My work schedule changes week to week" (correct path, advances). Continue for 2 more rounds along the correct path: "Why does that stop you cooking?" → "I can't commit to a weekly meal plan in advance" (advances) vs. a distractor "I don't like cooking" (feedback: "Priya's interviews didn't support this — stay with what she actually heard"). Final round reveals the root cause: "Rotating shifts make any pre-planned dinner routine unreliable" and labels it "Root Cause Found," contrasting it against the original symptom card still visible at the top.

Interactive controls:

  • Click a candidate answer to advance or receive corrective feedback
  • "Restart" button resets to the original symptom
  • Trail on the left is clickable to jump back to any earlier layer

Default parameters: Starts at the top-level symptom, no layers selected.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Store the drill-down as a small tree structure {text, children: [{text, correct, feedback}]}. Must remain fully readable on narrow (mobile) viewports — stack the trail above the current card rather than beside it below 600px width.

docs.title: Sizing the Problem: Severity, Frequency, and Urgency
docs.text:
Not every real, root-cause-confirmed problem deserves to anchor a venture. Three dimensions help size how much a problem actually matters to the customer who has it.

Dimension Question It Answers Priya's Finding Problem Severity How painful is this when it happens? High — skipped dinners affect the whole family's evening Problem Frequency How often does it happen? High — 3 to 5 nights per week on a rotating schedule Problem Urgency How soon does the customer want it solved? Moderate — a workaround exists (takeout), but it's expensive and unhealthy

Problem severity measures how painful or costly the problem is on any single occurrence it happens. Problem frequency measures how often that occurrence recurs for the target customer. Problem urgency measures how soon the customer wants a solution, independent of severity or frequency — a customer can feel a problem intensely and rarely (a flooded basement) or mildly but constantly (a slightly-too-small kitchen), and either combination can still justify a venture.

Multiply Severity by Frequency, Not Either Alone

Here's a shortcut: a mildly annoying problem that happens daily is often a stronger foundation than an intensely painful problem that happens once a year. Ask both questions, and don't let a dramatic severity score distract you from a weak frequency score.

docs.title: Writing the Problem Statement
docs.text:
With severity, frequency, and urgency in hand, problem framing is the choice of how to word a problem — which details to include, which customer language to borrow directly, and which angle to emphasize — since the same underlying problem can be framed narrowly or broadly with very different implications for the Solution block that follows. The finished output of that choice is the problem statement: the specific, written sentence describing the customer's problem that will sit in the canvas's Problem block, typically following a pattern like "[Target customer] struggles with [specific pain], caused by [root cause], which matters because [severity/frequency/urgency]."

When a founder has more than one candidate problem in view — which is common after a full round of interviews — problem prioritization is the deliberate act of ranking those candidate problems and choosing which one to pursue first, using the same severity, frequency, and urgency evidence rather than personal preference.

docs.title: Will They Actually Solve It?
docs.text:
A problem can be real, root-caused, frequent, and severe, and a customer can still never act to solve it. Willingness to solve describes whether a customer is actually motivated to spend money, time, or effort addressing a problem, as distinct from merely being bothered by it — plenty of real problems get quietly tolerated indefinitely. One specific and common reason a customer won't act is essential bills priority: the well-documented tendency for customers to direct limited money first toward non-negotiable obligations — rent, groceries, utilities, debt — before any discretionary spending on a problem that, however real, doesn't threaten their basic stability.

Annoying Is Not the Same as Solvable-For-Money

A common trap here is confirming a problem is real and then assuming willingness to solve automatically follows. It doesn't. Always ask directly: "What have you already tried, or paid for, to fix this?" If the honest answer is nothing, that problem may be competing with essential bills for a customer's limited money — and losing.

docs.title: From Problem to Solution
docs.text: Two final ideas carry this chapter's work into Chapter 6. Problem-solution fit is the degree to which a proposed solution actually addresses the validated root cause of a problem — as opposed to merely addressing its symptom, which the Five Whys work above exists to prevent. Problem discovery is the ongoing research process of finding and refining problem statements through direct contact with customers — not a one-time task completed in Session 1, but a habit that continues every time new field evidence complicates or sharpens what you thought you knew.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Before Chapter 6 turns this problem into an offer, hold onto how a problem gets defined:

  • Problem definition states, in testable terms, the customer pain behind a specific pain point — and stays a perceived problem until problem validation confirms it as a real problem.
  • Symptom vs. root cause thinking, using the Five Whys, distinguishes a surface complaint from the root cause, an unmet need, and the underlying job to be done.
  • Problem severity, frequency, and urgency size how much a problem matters; problem framing, the problem statement, and problem prioritization turn that sizing into the canvas's Problem block.
  • Willingness to solve — often limited by essential bills priority — determines whether a real problem will actually motivate action, and problem-solution fit is what keeps problem discovery honest as you move forward.

You Just Found the Real Problem

You can now tell a real problem from a perceived one, and a symptom from its root cause — the exact discipline that keeps a venture from solving the wrong thing well. Let's find out for real, starting with the Solution block in Chapter 6.

docs.title: Quiz: Defining the Real Problem
docs.text: Test your understanding of defining a validated customer problem with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. According to Chapter 5, what is a problem definition?
docs.text:
1. The practice of stating, in specific and falsifiable terms, the difficulty a target customer experiences that the venture intends to address
  2. A short slogan used to advertise the eventual solution to potential investors
  3. Any complaint a founder overhears from a stranger, whether or not it relates to the target customer
  4. The founder's best guess at what customers might want, updated only after the business launches
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A problem definition is the practice of stating, in specific and falsifiable terms, the difficulty your target customer experiences that your venture intends to address — specific enough that real evidence could confirm or contradict it. This is the second block on the canvas, and it only makes sense for a specific target customer, not people in general, which is why a vague observation like "people are busy" fails to qualify.

Concept Tested: Problem Definition

See: Glossary

docs.title: 2. How does the chapter define a pain point?
docs.text:
1. The general negative experience — frustration, cost, wasted time — that results from any unsolved problem
  2. One specific, nameable instance of a customer's pain, concrete enough to describe in a single sentence
  3. The finished sentence that will occupy the Problem block of the canvas
  4. A requirement that no existing option, including doing nothing, adequately satisfies
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A pain point is one specific, nameable instance of a customer's pain, concrete enough to describe in a single sentence — for example, Jordan's customer losing an unpaid afternoon of work to drive forty minutes each way for grooming drop-off. It is narrower than customer pain, which is the general negative experience behind it, and different from a problem statement or an unmet need.

Concept Tested: Pain Point

See: Glossary

docs.title: 3. Which statement best distinguishes customer pain from a pain point, as the chapter uses the terms?
docs.text:
1. Customer pain is always financial, while a pain point can be any type of frustration
  2. A pain point is a broad category, while customer pain is one specific instance inside it
  3. Customer pain is the negative experience a customer feels overall, while a pain point is one specific, single-sentence instance of that experience
  4. The two terms mean exactly the same thing and can be used interchangeably in a problem statement
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Customer pain is the negative experience — frustration, cost, wasted time, embarrassment, or risk — a customer feels as a direct result of an unsolved problem. A pain point narrows that broader experience down to one specific, nameable instance concrete enough to state in a single sentence. The two terms describe different levels of specificity, not interchangeable synonyms.

Concept Tested: Customer Pain

See: Glossary

docs.title: 4. Priya's interviewees kept saying "I don't have time to cook." Why does the chapter treat this as something other than the root cause?
docs.text:
1. Because Priya's interviewees were not part of her validated target customer segment
  2. Because the statement described a product feature rather than a customer experience
  3. Because the complaint was too severe to be believable without further evidence
  4. Because it was a surface-level symptom, and the root cause — schedule unpredictability — lay several layers beneath it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Priya's interviewees' first complaint, "I don't have time to cook," was a symptom — the surface-level statement offered first. Asking "why" repeatedly revealed the root cause: rotating shift schedules made any planned dinner routine unreliable, not a simple lack of hours. A solution built for the symptom alone would have missed what was actually producing the complaint.

Concept Tested: Root Cause

See: Glossary

docs.title: 5. Which sentence best follows the chapter's problem statement pattern of "[Target customer] struggles with [specific pain], caused by [root cause], which matters because [severity/frequency/urgency]"?
docs.text:
1. "Dog grooming should be more convenient for busy pet owners everywhere."
  2. "Jordan wants to build a mobile grooming business that customers will love."
  3. "Dog owners within 5 miles who don't own a car-friendly crate lose a half-day of income every time their dog needs grooming, because the nearest groomer requires in-person drop-off and pickup."
  4. "Most people are too busy to take their dog to the groomer on time."
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. This sentence follows the chapter's pattern — target customer, specific pain, root cause, and why it matters — using Jordan's actual refined problem statement: dog owners within 5 miles losing a half-day of income because the nearest groomer requires in-person drop-off and pickup. The other options are vague aspirations or founder-centered statements, not falsifiable problem statements.

Concept Tested: Problem Statement

See: Glossary

docs.title: 6. What does problem severity measure?
docs.text:
1. How painful or costly the problem is on any single occurrence when it happens
  2. How many times per week the problem tends to recur for the customer
  3. How soon the customer wants the problem solved once it is confirmed real
  4. How many competing alternatives already exist for solving the problem
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Problem severity measures how painful or costly the problem is on any single occurrence — independent of how often it happens or how soon the customer wants it fixed. A flooded basement is an example of high severity paired with low frequency, showing severity is its own distinct dimension from problem frequency and problem urgency.

Concept Tested: Problem Severity

See: Glossary

docs.title: 7. Priya found her target customers faced their dinner problem 3 to 5 nights a week on a rotating schedule. Which dimension does this finding measure?
docs.text:
1. Problem severity, because it reflects how disruptive each missed dinner is
  2. Problem urgency, because it reflects how soon customers want a fix
  3. Willingness to solve, because it reflects how motivated customers are to pay
  4. Problem frequency, because it reflects how often the problem recurs for the customer
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Problem frequency measures how often the problem recurs for the target customer. Priya's finding that the dinner problem struck 3 to 5 nights per week on a rotating schedule is a frequency measurement, distinct from severity (how painful each occurrence is) and urgency (how soon the customer wants it solved).

Concept Tested: Problem Frequency

See: Glossary

docs.title: 8. A founder finishes a round of interviews with three candidate problems in view. What does the chapter say problem prioritization requires the founder to do?
docs.text:
1. Pursue whichever problem was mentioned first in the very first interview
  2. Rank the candidate problems using severity, frequency, and urgency evidence, then choose which to pursue first
  3. Build a small solution for all three problems simultaneously to see which one sells
  4. Defer the decision until every possible customer has been interviewed at least once
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Problem prioritization is the deliberate act of ranking candidate problems and choosing which one to pursue first, using severity, frequency, and urgency evidence rather than personal preference or the order problems happened to surface. Founders commonly surface more than one candidate problem after a full round of interviews, making this ranking step necessary.

Concept Tested: Problem Prioritization

See: Glossary

docs.title: 9. What makes a problem a "real problem" rather than merely a perceived one, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. It has been described in a formal problem statement using the canvas's exact wording
  2. It affects a large enough number of people to matter to investors
  3. A founder is personally confident, based on outside research, that it exists
  4. Customers actually experience it and can describe it from their own lived frustration when asked directly, confirmed through evidence
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A real problem is one that customers actually experience and can describe from their own lived frustration when asked directly, confirmed through evidence rather than founder intuition. This distinguishes it from a perceived problem, which a founder believes exists based on logic or outside research but has not yet confirmed with the actual target customer.

Concept Tested: Real Problem

See: Glossary

docs.title: 10. How does the chapter define a perceived problem?
docs.text:
1. A problem that has already failed a round of problem validation and should be discarded
  2. A problem invented purely for the purpose of a pitch competition
  3. A problem a founder believes customers have, based on logic, outside research, or personal experience, that hasn't yet been confirmed by talking to the target customer
  4. A problem that only exists in a market survey and has no basis in individual experience
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A perceived problem is one a founder believes customers have, based on logic, outside research, or personal experience, that has not yet been confirmed by talking to the actual target customer. The chapter stresses that every real problem starts out perceived — the mistake is building a solution around it before validation, not holding the perception itself.

Concept Tested: Perceived Problem

See: Glossary

docs.title: 11. Jordan initially assumed, without asking anyone, that dog owners were frustrated by drop-off grooming. What step would the chapter say Jordan needs to take before treating that assumption as a real problem?
docs.text:
1. Problem validation — testing the perceived problem against real customer conversations and behavior
  2. Problem framing — deciding which words to use when describing the problem
  3. Problem prioritization — ranking it against other candidate problems Jordan has noticed
  4. Solution testing — building a small offer and seeing whether anyone buys it
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Problem validation is the process of testing a perceived problem against real customer conversations and behavior to confirm whether it is genuinely felt, exactly as urgently as assumed. Jordan's untested assumption about drop-off frustration remains perceived until real customers confirm it directly — logic and outside research alone cannot make a perceived problem real.

Concept Tested: Problem Validation

See: Glossary

docs.title: 12. A founder builds a solution that neatly resolves a customer's very first complaint but leaves the deeper, validated cause of that complaint completely untouched. Which concept explains what is missing?
docs.text:
1. Problem framing, because the founder chose the wrong words to describe the problem
  2. Problem-solution fit, because the solution addresses the symptom rather than the validated root cause
  3. Problem urgency, because the founder moved too slowly to help the customer
  4. Essential bills priority, because the customer cannot afford the proposed solution
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Problem-solution fit is the degree to which a proposed solution actually addresses the validated root cause of a problem, as opposed to merely addressing its symptom. A solution that resolves only the first complaint a customer voices, while leaving the deeper cause untouched, has poor problem-solution fit even if it feels responsive in the moment.

Concept Tested: Problem-Solution Fit

See: Glossary

docs.title: 13. In the Five Whys drill-down, Priya's interviewees first said "I don't have time to cook," and only after repeated "why" questions did "rotating shifts make any pre-planned dinner routine unreliable" emerge. What discipline does this drill-down illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Problem prioritization, because it ranks candidate problems by severity and frequency
  2. Problem validation, because it confirms whether a perceived problem is genuinely felt
  3. Symptom vs. root cause, the discipline of not stopping at the first explanation a customer offers
  4. Problem discovery, the ongoing habit of finding and refining problem statements over time
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Symptom vs. root cause is the discipline of not stopping at the first explanation a customer offers, because a solution built for a symptom often leaves the root cause untouched. The repeated "why" technique in Priya's drill-down — sometimes called the Five Whys — is exactly this discipline applied step by step until the answer stops changing.

Concept Tested: Symptom Vs Root Cause

See: Glossary

docs.title: 14. How does the chapter define an unmet need?
docs.text:
1. A pain point so severe that a customer would pay any price to resolve it
  2. A customer requirement that no current option — including doing nothing — adequately satisfies, whether or not the customer has put it into words
  3. A feature a founder decides to build regardless of customer feedback
  4. The written sentence describing a problem that will sit in the canvas's Problem block
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An unmet need is a customer requirement that no current option — including doing nothing — adequately satisfies, whether or not the customer has ever put it into words. It is closely related to, but distinct from, a job to be done, which reframes the same territory around the function or outcome the customer is trying to accomplish.

Concept Tested: Unmet Need

See: Glossary

docs.title: 15. Which framing below correctly expresses Priya's situation as a job to be done, rather than as a product?
docs.text:
1. "Priya should sell a subscription meal-kit service to busy families."
  2. "Priya's customers want a well-known meal-kit brand delivered to their door."
  3. "Priya's customers are frustrated because they don't have time to cook."
  4. "Priya's customers are fundamentally trying to get a nutritious dinner on the table with zero advance planning."
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A job to be done reframes the question around function rather than feature: the underlying task or outcome a customer is fundamentally trying to accomplish, independent of any particular product. Framing Priya's customers as wanting "a nutritious dinner on the table with zero advance planning" captures the job, rather than describing a specific product like a meal kit.

Concept Tested: Job To Be Done

See: Glossary

docs.title: 16. Why does the chapter treat problem framing as a meaningful choice rather than a neutral formality?
docs.text:
1. Because the same underlying problem can be worded narrowly or broadly, with very different implications for the Solution block that follows
  2. Because only one legally acceptable wording exists for any given problem statement
  3. Because customers refuse to participate in interviews unless the framing is finalized first
  4. Because framing determines the price a customer will ultimately be willing to pay
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Problem framing is the choice of how to word a problem — which details to include, which customer language to borrow directly, and which angle to emphasize. Because the same underlying problem can be framed narrowly or broadly, that choice carries real implications for how the Solution block gets designed in the next chapter.

Concept Tested: Problem Framing

See: Glossary

docs.title: 17. What does problem urgency measure, as distinct from severity and frequency?
docs.text:
1. How costly the problem is on any single occurrence when it happens
  2. How often the problem recurs for the target customer
  3. How many direct competitors already address the same problem
  4. How soon the customer wants a solution, independent of severity or frequency
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Problem urgency measures how soon the customer wants a solution, independent of severity or frequency. A customer can feel a problem intensely but rarely, like a flooded basement, or mildly but constantly, like a slightly-too-small kitchen — either combination can still justify a venture, which is why urgency is tracked as its own dimension.

Concept Tested: Problem Urgency

See: Glossary

docs.title: 18. A customer confirms a problem is real, severe, and frequent, but has never spent any money or effort trying to fix it. What does the chapter say a founder should check next?
docs.text:
1. Whether the problem has been framed narrowly enough for a clear problem statement
  2. Whether a direct competitor already offers a solution to the same problem
  3. Willingness to solve — whether the customer is actually motivated to spend money, time, or effort, not just bothered by the problem
  4. Problem discovery — whether enough interviews have been conducted to confirm the finding
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Willingness to solve describes whether a customer is actually motivated to spend money, time, or effort addressing a problem, as distinct from merely being bothered by it. A problem can be real, severe, and frequent, and a customer can still never act on it — which is exactly why the chapter treats willingness to solve as a separate check.

Concept Tested: Willingness To Solve

See: Glossary

docs.title: 19. A customer agrees a problem is real and even mildly bothersome, but says they've never paid for anything to address it because "rent and groceries come first." Which concept best explains this pattern?
docs.text:
1. Problem urgency, because the customer does not want the problem solved quickly
  2. Essential bills priority — the tendency to direct limited money toward non-negotiable obligations before any discretionary spending
  3. Problem-solution fit, because no available solution matches the customer's root cause
  4. Perceived problem, because the customer has not actually experienced the difficulty firsthand
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Essential bills priority is the well-documented tendency for customers to direct limited money first toward non-negotiable obligations — rent, groceries, utilities, debt — before any discretionary spending on a problem that, however real, doesn't threaten their basic stability. It is one specific, common reason a confirmed real problem still fails to produce willingness to solve.

Concept Tested: Essential Bills Priority

See: Glossary

docs.title: 20. After finishing her first round of interviews, Priya keeps talking to new customers each week, and her problem statement keeps getting sharper as a result. Which concept does this ongoing habit represent?
docs.text:
1. Problem discovery — the ongoing research process of finding and refining problem statements through direct customer contact
  2. Problem prioritization — ranking multiple candidate problems against each other
  3. Problem validation — a one-time test of whether a perceived problem is genuinely felt
  4. Problem framing — deciding which words and angle to use in the problem statement
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Problem discovery is the ongoing research process of finding and refining problem statements through direct contact with customers — not a one-time task completed in an early session, but a habit that continues every time new field evidence complicates or sharpens what the founder thought they knew. Priya's continuing interviews are this habit in practice.

Concept Tested: Problem Discovery

See: Glossary

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Shows how to turn a validated problem into a minimum viable offer, iterating on solution scope and clarity before any customer interviews take place.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 20 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Solution Definition 2276 Initial Offer 13 Minimum Viable Offer 6 Product Offering 6 Service Offering 6 What You Offer 5 Solution Fit 5 Feature Vs Benefit 5 Offer Design 4 Solution Iteration 4 Solution Scope 4 Draft Business Idea 3 Solution Refinement 3 Core Offering 3 Value Delivery 2 Solution Simplicity 2 Solution Assumption 2 Offer Clarity 1 Solution Testing 1 Solution Pivot 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The CO.STARTERS Canvas Framework
  • Chapter 5: Defining the Real Problem

docs.title: The Third Block: What Will You Actually Offer?
docs.text:
Chapter 5 ended with a validated, root-caused problem statement. This chapter turns that statement into the Solution block — what you will actually build, sell, or deliver. The instinct at this point is to design something impressive. This chapter argues, deliberately, for the opposite instinct: design something small enough to test before your first customer interview, refined only by evidence afterward.

Designing Just Enough

This chapter is going to keep pulling you back toward "smaller" every time your instinct says "more complete." That's not caution for its own sake — it's how you get a real answer from a real customer sooner instead of later. Let's find out for real!

docs.title: From Root Cause to Draft Solution
docs.text:
Solution definition is the practice of describing, in specific terms, what a venture will actually offer to address a validated problem — the third block on the canvas, and the first one where a founder starts building rather than just researching. A strong solution definition traces directly back to the root cause identified in Chapter 5, not merely to the symptom a customer first mentioned.

The earliest form this takes is a draft business idea: a rough, unpolished first pass at what the solution might be, written down specifically so it can be tested and changed rather than kept vague and unfalsifiable. That draft answers what you offer: the specific plain-language description of the product or service a customer receives — the CO.STARTERS Canvas's own phrasing for this block's guiding question. Jordan's draft business idea reads: "Mobile dog grooming, delivered at the customer's home, booked by text message, paid at time of service."

docs.title: Products, Services, and Your Core Offering
docs.text:
Every draft solution takes one of two basic shapes, or some blend of both. A product offering is a solution delivered as a tangible or standardized item the customer owns or consumes, produced once and sold repeatedly with little variation. A service offering is a solution delivered as a performed activity, customized in the moment to a specific customer's situation, and consumed as it's delivered rather than owned afterward. Jordan's grooming is a service offering; a bagged batch of pre-made dog treats sold at the same driveway visit would be a product offering.

Most real ventures center on one of these two, called the core offering: the single primary product or service a venture is built around, as distinct from any secondary add-ons that might come later. Naming a clear core offering matters because an early-stage venture with three different core offerings usually has zero well-tested offerings — the resources meant to validate one thing get split three ways instead.

docs.title: Keeping the First Offer Small
docs.text:
A common early mistake is designing a solution meant to satisfy every version of the problem for every version of the customer at once. The remedy is a minimum viable offer: the smallest, simplest version of a solution capable of genuinely solving the core problem for a target customer, containing only what is essential to test whether the underlying idea works — no polish, no edge cases handled, no nice-to-haves. Solution scope is the deliberate boundary a founder draws around what the offer will and will not include, and solution simplicity is the discipline of keeping that scope as narrow as possible without breaking the offer's ability to actually solve the core problem.

That narrowed, testable version becomes the initial offer: the specific, concrete version of the minimum viable offer that a founder actually presents to real customers during the very first round of field testing. For the initial offer to do its job, it also needs offer clarity: the property of being stated so plainly and specifically that a customer immediately understands what they'd be getting and for how much, with no follow-up questions required just to understand the pitch. Jordan's initial offer: "A single dog wash and brush-out, at your home, for $40, this week." Not the full grooming menu — one clear, bookable thing.

The Goal Isn't the Best Offer — It's the Fastest Honest Answer

Notice the shift in what "good" means here. A minimum viable offer isn't a lesser version of the real business — it's a deliberately incomplete tool whose entire purpose is producing a fast, honest yes-or-no from a real customer. Completeness is a later problem, once you know the core idea works.

Before trying the slider below, notice what happens to an offer as scope shrinks: some features disappear entirely, others turn out to have been essential all along. The interactive tool below lets you adjust Jordan's offer's scope and see which pieces survive.

docs.title: Diagram: Minimum Viable Offer Slider
docs.text:
Minimum Viable Offer Slider

Type: microsim sim-id: minimum-viable-offer-slider Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: apply

Learning objective: Learners adjust an offer's scope using a slider and observe which features of a draft business idea are essential to the core offering versus removable, applying the concept of a minimum viable offer to a concrete example.

Canvas layout:

  • Top: a slider labeled "Offer Scope" ranging from 0 (bare minimum) to 100 (full imagined business)
  • Below: a card showing Jordan's full imagined offer as a checklist of 8 features, each with a threshold value at which it appears/disappears as the slider moves
  • Side panel: a running label reading "Minimum Viable Offer" (0-25), "Initial Offer" (26-50), "Established Offering" (51-100)

Feature list with scope thresholds (features become visible above their threshold):

  • "Basic wash and brush-out" — threshold 0 (always visible, the essential core)
  • "At the customer's home" — threshold 0 (always visible, the essential core)
  • "Text-message booking" — threshold 10
  • "Nail trim add-on" — threshold 30
  • "Multiple dog breeds/sizes supported" — threshold 40
  • "Online booking calendar" — threshold 55
  • "Flea/tick treatment option" — threshold 65
  • "Branded van and uniform" — threshold 85

Interactive controls:

  • Drag the slider; features above the current threshold appear checked, features below fade to gray
  • At scope values 0-25, panel displays: "This is a Minimum Viable Offer — just enough to test the core problem"
  • Reset button returns slider to 0

Default parameters: Slider starts at 15 (showing "Basic wash and brush-out," "At the customer's home," and "Text-message booking" — Jordan's actual initial offer).

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Store features as an array of objects {label, threshold}; render checklist by comparing each threshold to the current slider value. Must remain fully readable on narrow (mobile) viewports — stack the checklist below the slider.

When in Doubt, Cut It in Half Again

Here's a shortcut: whatever offer you've drafted, ask "what would this look like with half the features?" Then ask again. Most founders land on a genuinely minimum offer only after cutting twice past the point that first felt uncomfortably small.

docs.title: Feature vs Benefit, and Delivering Real Value
docs.text: As you decide what stays in scope, it helps to separate two different things people often blur together. Feature vs. benefit is the distinction between what a solution technically does or includes (a feature) and what positive outcome the customer actually experiences as a result (a benefit) — "text-message booking" is a feature; "no phone tag, no waiting on hold" is the benefit it produces. Offer design is the overall process of shaping which features, format, and terms make up a solution, guided by which benefits actually matter to the target customer rather than which features are easiest or most interesting to build. Value delivery is the mechanism by which a customer actually receives that benefit — not just what's promised, but how and when it's concretely handed over. Finally, solution fit measures how well the designed offer actually matches the validated problem and target customer from the two previous chapters, rather than matching what a founder personally finds exciting to build.

docs.title: Every Solution Starts as an Assumption
docs.text:
Just as Chapter 4 established that a customer definition begins as a customer assumption, a draft solution carries its own version. A solution assumption is an unverified belief that a specific offer will actually solve the customer's validated problem well enough that they'll choose it — true by hope, not yet by evidence. Solution testing is the process, covered in full in Chapter 10, of exposing that assumption to real customer behavior to find out whether it holds.

Testing It In Your Head Doesn't Count

A common trap here is "testing" a solution assumption by imagining how customers would react, rather than actually offering it to one. The fix: treat every solution assumption as untested until a real person has said yes or no to the real initial offer — not a description of it.

docs.title: Refining, Iterating, or Pivoting
docs.text: A first initial offer is rarely the last version. Solution iteration is the repeated cycle of adjusting an offer based on field evidence, then testing the adjusted version again — the same evidence-based-decision-making habit from Chapter 1, applied specifically to the Solution block. Solution refinement describes the smaller, incremental adjustments within that cycle — tightening scope, clarifying the offer, adding one validated feature back in. A solution pivot is the larger move: abandoning the current solution approach entirely in favor of a substantially different one, made when evidence shows the current direction can't be refined into something that works, only replaced.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Before Chapter 7 looks at what customers use instead of you, hold onto how an offer gets built:

  • Solution definition turns a validated problem into a draft business idea answering what you offer, expressed as a product offering, a service offering, or both, centered on one clear core offering.
  • A minimum viable offer, bounded by deliberate solution scope and solution simplicity, becomes the actual initial offer — made testable by real offer clarity.
  • Feature vs. benefit thinking, sound offer design, and genuine value delivery determine solution fit with your validated customer and problem.
  • Every offer starts as a solution assumption, resolved only through real solution testing — after which solution iteration, solution refinement, or a full solution pivot takes it forward.

You Just Designed a Testable Offer

You now have an offer small enough to test honestly and clear enough that a stranger would understand it in one sentence — that's exactly the bar this chapter set out to clear. Let's find out for real, starting with what customers use instead of you in Chapter 7.

docs.title: Quiz: Designing the Solution & Initial Offer
docs.text: Test your understanding of designing a testable initial offer with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How does the chapter define solution definition?
docs.text:
1. A polished, investor-ready pitch describing every feature a venture will eventually build
  2. The practice of describing, in specific terms, what a venture will actually offer to address a validated problem
  3. A marketing slogan chosen to make the product sound appealing to a broad audience
  4. The final signed agreement between a founder and their first paying customer
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Solution definition is the practice of describing, in specific terms, what a venture will actually offer to address a validated problem — the third block on the canvas, and the first one where a founder starts building rather than researching. A strong solution definition traces back to the root cause identified in the Problem block, not to a polished pitch or slogan.

Concept Tested: Solution Definition

See: Glossary

docs.title: 2. Which statement best explains what makes something an initial offer rather than just a minimum viable offer?
docs.text:
1. An initial offer includes every feature a founder eventually plans to build, while a minimum viable offer excludes them
  2. The two terms are identical and can be used interchangeably at any stage of testing
  3. An initial offer is the specific, concrete version of the minimum viable offer that a founder actually presents to real customers during the first round of field testing
  4. An initial offer is only used once a venture already has paying customers
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An initial offer is the specific, concrete version of the minimum viable offer that a founder actually presents to real customers during the very first round of field testing. Jordan's initial offer — a single dog wash and brush-out, at home, for $40, this week — narrows the broader minimum viable offer concept into one testable, bookable thing.

Concept Tested: Initial Offer

See: Glossary

docs.title: 3. What is a minimum viable offer, as the chapter defines it?
docs.text:
1. The smallest, simplest version of a solution capable of genuinely solving the core problem, containing only what is essential to test whether the idea works
  2. A discounted version of the full product offered only to a venture's very first customers
  3. Any offer priced below what competitors currently charge for a similar solution
  4. The final, polished version of an offer after several rounds of solution iteration
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A minimum viable offer is the smallest, simplest version of a solution capable of genuinely solving the core problem for a target customer, containing only what is essential to test whether the underlying idea works — no polish, no edge cases, no nice-to-haves. It is not simply a discount or a final polished product.

Concept Tested: Minimum Viable Offer

See: Glossary

docs.title: 4. Which pairing correctly distinguishes a product offering from a service offering, using Jordan's example?
docs.text:
1. Both a dog wash and a bag of pre-made treats are product offerings, because both involve a physical dog
  2. A product offering is always more expensive than a service offering
  3. Mobile dog grooming is a product offering because it is delivered at the customer's home
  4. A bagged batch of pre-made dog treats is a product offering — a tangible item produced once and sold repeatedly — while the grooming itself is a service offering
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A product offering is a tangible or standardized item the customer owns or consumes, produced once and sold repeatedly with little variation — like Jordan's bagged pre-made dog treats. Jordan's grooming itself is a service offering: a performed activity customized in the moment and consumed as it's delivered, not owned afterward.

Concept Tested: Product Offering

See: Glossary

docs.title: 5. Why does the chapter classify Jordan's mobile grooming as a service offering rather than a product offering?
docs.text:
1. Because it is delivered as a performed activity, customized in the moment to a specific customer's dog, and consumed as it's delivered rather than owned afterward
  2. Because it is produced once in a factory and then sold repeatedly with little variation
  3. Because customers can return it for a refund if they are unsatisfied with the result
  4. Because it does not require any direct interaction between Jordan and the customer
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A service offering is delivered as a performed activity, customized in the moment to a specific customer's situation, and consumed as it's delivered rather than owned afterward. Jordan's mobile grooming fits this exactly — each visit is performed live for a specific dog, unlike a standardized item produced once and sold repeatedly.

Concept Tested: Service Offering

See: Glossary

docs.title: 6. In the CO.STARTERS Canvas's own phrasing, what question does the "what you offer" idea answer?
docs.text:
1. How much the solution will cost the customer to purchase
  2. The specific plain-language description of the product or service a customer receives
  3. Which competitors already provide something similar in the market
  4. How the founder plans to advertise the solution to strangers
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. "What you offer" is the CO.STARTERS Canvas's own phrasing for the Solution block's guiding question: the specific plain-language description of the product or service a customer receives. Jordan's draft business idea — mobile dog grooming, delivered at home, booked by text, paid at time of service — answers exactly this question.

Concept Tested: What You Offer

See: Glossary

docs.title: 7. A founder designs an offer they personally find exciting to build, but it only loosely matches the validated problem and target customer from earlier chapters. What is missing?
docs.text:
1. Offer clarity, because the pitch is too complicated for a stranger to understand
  2. Solution simplicity, because the offer includes too many features at once
  3. Value delivery, because the benefit is not being handed over on time
  4. Solution fit, because the offer needs to match the validated problem and customer rather than the founder's personal interest
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Solution fit measures how well the designed offer actually matches the validated problem and target customer from the previous chapters, rather than matching what a founder personally finds exciting to build. An offer built around a founder's own enthusiasm, without checking it against the validated problem and customer, has weak solution fit even if it is well executed.

Concept Tested: Solution Fit

See: Glossary

docs.title: 8. Jordan's offer includes text-message booking. Which statement correctly applies the feature-vs-benefit distinction to this detail?
docs.text:
1. "Text-message booking" is the benefit, and "no phone tag, no waiting on hold" is the feature
  2. Both phrases describe the same feature, worded two different ways for marketing purposes
  3. "Text-message booking" is the feature — what the solution technically includes — and "no phone tag, no waiting on hold" is the benefit customers actually experience
  4. Neither phrase qualifies as a feature or a benefit; both describe the venture's core offering
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Feature vs. benefit distinguishes what a solution technically does or includes (a feature) from the positive outcome the customer actually experiences as a result (a benefit). "Text-message booking" is the feature; "no phone tag, no waiting on hold" is the benefit it produces for the customer — the two are related but not the same thing.

Concept Tested: Feature Vs Benefit

See: Glossary

docs.title: 9. What guides offer design, according to the chapter, when a founder decides which features, format, and terms to include?
docs.text:
1. Whichever features are easiest or most interesting for the founder to build first
  2. Which benefits actually matter to the target customer, rather than which features are easiest to build
  3. The exact feature set already offered by the venture's closest direct competitor
  4. A fixed checklist of features required by every minimum viable offer regardless of the problem
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Offer design is the overall process of shaping which features, format, and terms make up a solution, guided by which benefits actually matter to the target customer — not by which features are easiest or most interesting for the founder to build. This keeps the offer anchored to customer value rather than founder convenience.

Concept Tested: Offer Design

See: Glossary

docs.title: 10. After Jordan's first initial offer gets field-tested, Jordan adjusts the offer based on what customers said and tests the new version again. Which concept describes this repeated cycle?
docs.text:
1. Solution refinement, because it only covers small, incremental wording changes
  2. Solution pivot, because Jordan abandoned the original approach entirely
  3. Solution assumption, because Jordan is still guessing what customers want
  4. Solution iteration, the repeated cycle of adjusting an offer based on field evidence and testing the adjusted version again
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Solution iteration is the repeated cycle of adjusting an offer based on field evidence, then testing the adjusted version again — the same evidence-based-decision-making habit applied specifically to the Solution block. It is a broader, ongoing cycle, distinct from solution refinement, which describes the smaller adjustments made within each iteration.

Concept Tested: Solution Iteration

See: Glossary

docs.title: 11. How does the chapter define solution scope?
docs.text:
1. The deliberate boundary a founder draws around what the offer will and will not include
  2. The total number of customers a venture hopes to serve within its first year
  3. The geographic area within which a founder is willing to deliver a service
  4. The list of every feature a founder might build once funding becomes available
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Solution scope is the deliberate boundary a founder draws around what the offer will and will not include. Drawing this boundary intentionally — rather than letting the offer grow to satisfy every possible version of the problem — is what makes a minimum viable offer possible in the first place.

Concept Tested: Solution Scope

See: Glossary

docs.title: 12. What is a draft business idea, as the chapter uses the term?
docs.text:
1. A legally binding business plan submitted to investors before any customer interviews occur
  2. The final, most polished description of a venture's offering after solution testing is complete
  3. A rough, unpolished first pass at what the solution might be, written down specifically so it can be tested and changed
  4. A list of every competitor's offering, used as a template for the founder's own solution
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A draft business idea is a rough, unpolished first pass at what the solution might be, written down specifically so it can be tested and changed rather than kept vague and unfalsifiable. Jordan's draft — mobile dog grooming, delivered at home, booked by text, paid at time of service — is an early, testable statement, not a finished business plan.

Concept Tested: Draft Business Idea

See: Glossary

docs.title: 13. Jordan tightens the wording of the initial offer and adds back one previously cut feature after customers say they'd like it. Which concept best describes this specific adjustment?
docs.text:
1. Solution pivot, because Jordan is abandoning mobile grooming for a different approach
  2. Draft business idea, because Jordan is writing the very first version of the offer
  3. Solution assumption, because Jordan has not yet tested the adjustment with customers
  4. Solution refinement — the smaller, incremental adjustment within the iteration cycle, such as tightening scope or adding one validated feature back in
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Solution refinement describes the smaller, incremental adjustments made within the solution iteration cycle — tightening scope, clarifying the offer, or adding one validated feature back in. Jordan tightening wording and restoring a single customer-requested feature is exactly this scale of adjustment, distinct from the larger break of a solution pivot.

Concept Tested: Solution Refinement

See: Glossary

docs.title: 14. Why does the chapter caution against a venture having three different core offerings at once?
docs.text:
1. Because customers are legally required to choose only one offering per venture
  2. Because the resources meant to validate one thing get split three ways instead, usually leaving zero well-tested offerings
  3. Because product offerings and service offerings cannot legally coexist within the same venture
  4. Because a minimum viable offer can only ever contain a single feature
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter warns that an early-stage venture with three different core offerings usually ends up with zero well-tested offerings, because the limited resources meant to validate one thing get split three ways instead. Naming one clear core offering — the single primary product or service the venture is built around — keeps testing focused.

Concept Tested: Core Offering

See: Glossary

docs.title: 15. Jordan promises customers "no phone tag, no waiting on hold," and then actually confirms every booking within minutes by text. Which concept does the actual, concrete confirmation represent?
docs.text:
1. Offer clarity, because the pitch is stated plainly with no follow-up questions needed
  2. Feature vs. benefit, because it distinguishes what the offer includes from what it produces
  3. Value delivery — the mechanism by which a customer actually receives the promised benefit, not just what's promised
  4. Solution scope, because it defines the boundary of what the offer will include
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Value delivery is the mechanism by which a customer actually receives a promised benefit — not just what's promised, but how and when it's concretely handed over. Jordan's fast text confirmation is the concrete delivery of the "no phone tag" benefit, turning a promise made in the pitch into something the customer actually experiences.

Concept Tested: Value Delivery

See: Glossary

docs.title: 16. How does solution simplicity relate to solution scope, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Solution simplicity is the discipline of keeping scope as narrow as possible without breaking the offer's ability to actually solve the core problem
  2. Solution simplicity means removing every feature from an offer, including the ones essential to solving the core problem
  3. Solution simplicity only applies to product offerings, never to service offerings
  4. Solution simplicity is a synonym for offer clarity and does not involve scope at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Solution simplicity is the discipline of keeping solution scope as narrow as possible without breaking the offer's ability to actually solve the core problem. The two concepts work together: scope defines the boundary, and simplicity is the discipline of pushing that boundary as tight as it can go while still solving the problem.

Concept Tested: Solution Simplicity

See: Glossary

docs.title: 17. A founder is confident their offer will solve the customer's problem because they've imagined several scenarios in their head, but no real customer has said yes or no yet. What does the chapter call this belief?
docs.text:
1. Draft business idea, because it is still an early, unpolished version of the offer
  2. Solution fit, because it has not yet been checked against the validated problem
  3. Solution assumption — an unverified belief that a specific offer will solve the customer's problem, true by hope rather than evidence
  4. Offer clarity, because the founder has not yet stated the offer plainly enough
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A solution assumption is an unverified belief that a specific offer will actually solve the customer's validated problem well enough that they'll choose it — true by hope, not yet by evidence. Imagining customer reactions does not resolve a solution assumption; only exposing it to real customer behavior, through solution testing, can do that.

Concept Tested: Solution Assumption

See: Glossary

docs.title: 18. Which version of Jordan's pitch best demonstrates offer clarity?
docs.text:
1. "A single dog wash and brush-out, at your home, for $40, this week."
  2. "Comprehensive at-home pet care solutions tailored to your unique needs."
  3. "Mobile grooming services available, pricing varies depending on several factors."
  4. "We handle everything your dog could possibly need, whenever you need it."
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Offer clarity is the property of being stated so plainly and specifically that a customer immediately understands what they'd be getting and for how much, with no follow-up questions required. Jordan's "single dog wash and brush-out, at your home, for $40, this week" states exactly what, where, and how much — unlike the vaguer, jargon-filled alternatives.

Concept Tested: Offer Clarity

See: Glossary

docs.title: 19. A founder has a solution assumption but has only tested it by imagining how customers might react. What does the chapter say still needs to happen before the assumption can be considered resolved?
docs.text:
1. Solution refinement, to tighten the offer's scope before any customer sees it
  2. Offer design, to decide which features and terms belong in the solution
  3. Solution iteration, to adjust the offer repeatedly without customer contact
  4. Solution testing — exposing the assumption to real customer behavior, since imagining a reaction does not count as evidence
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Solution testing is the process of exposing a solution assumption to real customer behavior to find out whether it holds. Imagining how customers would react is explicitly called out as not counting — the chapter insists every solution assumption stays untested until a real person has said yes or no to the real initial offer.

Concept Tested: Solution Testing

See: Glossary

docs.title: 20. After months of testing, evidence shows Jordan's mobile-grooming approach cannot be refined into something that works, so Jordan abandons it for a completely different approach: selling grooming supplies online instead. Which concept describes this move?
docs.text:
1. Solution refinement, because it is a small, incremental adjustment to the existing offer
  2. Solution pivot — abandoning the current solution approach entirely in favor of a substantially different one
  3. Solution iteration, because Jordan is testing an adjusted version of the same offer again
  4. Solution assumption, because Jordan has not yet gathered any evidence about the new approach
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A solution pivot is the larger move of abandoning the current solution approach entirely in favor of a substantially different one, made when evidence shows the current direction can't be refined into something that works, only replaced. Switching from mobile grooming to selling supplies online is a full change of approach, not an incremental refinement.

Concept Tested: Solution Pivot

See: Glossary

docs.text: Maps how customers currently solve the problem today, from direct competitors to do-nothing alternatives, to reveal genuine gaps in the market.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 18 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Alternative Solution 657 Competitor 11 Competitive Landscape 6 Current Workaround 5 Substitute Solution 5 Direct Competitor 5 Indirect Competitor 4 Do-Nothing Alternative 4 Competitive Analysis 4 Market Gap 3 Competitive Positioning 3 Differentiation 3 Competitive Research 2 Existing Solution 2 Status Quo 2 Competitive Landscape Mapping 1 Alternative Assessment 1 Competitive Intelligence 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The CO.STARTERS Canvas Framework
  • Chapter 6: Designing the Solution & Initial Offer

docs.title: The Fourth Block: What Are They Doing Instead of You?
docs.text:
Chapter 6 gave you an initial offer. Before assuming a customer will choose it, this chapter asks an uncomfortable but necessary question: what are they doing right now, without you? Nobody encounters a validated problem and simply waits, undecided, until your venture launches. They're already coping somehow — and understanding exactly how is what the Alternatives block is for.

Meet the Competition You Didn't Know You Had

Most first-time founders think "I don't really have competitors" — and they're almost always wrong, just not in the way they expect. By the end of this chapter you'll know exactly who and what you're actually up against. Let's find out for real!

docs.title: What Counts as an Alternative
docs.text:
An alternative solution is anything a target customer currently uses, does, or chooses instead of your proposed offer to address their problem — a category far broader than "other companies selling something similar." This is the fourth canvas block, and it's frequently the one founders fill in too narrowly, because the word "competitor" makes people think only of rival businesses.

Two ideas widen that view. An existing solution is any product, service, or method — commercial or not — currently available to a customer for addressing their problem. The status quo is simply how the customer currently lives with the problem overall, encompassing every existing solution they use, ignore, or tolerate. For Jordan's target customer, the status quo isn't one groomer — it's some combination of a booked-solid salon, a bottle of dry shampoo, and quietly accepting a slightly smelly dog between visits.

docs.title: The Do-Nothing Alternative and the Current Workaround
docs.text:
The single most overlooked alternative in this entire chapter is the simplest one. The do-nothing alternative is the option of a customer simply continuing to tolerate the problem, unsolved, rather than adopting any solution at all — and it is, for most problems, the actual default competitor a venture has to beat. A current workaround is any informal, imperfect method a customer has assembled on their own to partially address the problem without a dedicated solution — Priya's interviewees' current workaround for dinner wasn't a competing meal-kit company; it was a rotating mix of takeout, cereal for dinner, and a freezer full of half-used ingredients.

Your Real Competitor Is Usually 'Nothing,' Not a Rival

Notice the shift this creates: the question isn't "how do I beat the other dog groomer" — it's "how do I beat forty minutes of driving and quietly not getting the dog groomed." The do-nothing alternative is almost always the toughest competitor in the room, because it costs the customer nothing to keep choosing it.

docs.title: Direct, Indirect, and Substitute Competitors
docs.text:
Once the full status quo is in view, it helps to sort the alternatives inside it. A competitor is any existing solution — business, product, or workaround — that a target customer might choose over your offer. A direct competitor solves the same problem for the same target customer using essentially the same approach — another mobile dog groomer, for Jordan. An indirect competitor solves the same underlying problem but through a meaningfully different approach — a traditional storefront groomer that requires drop-off, for instance. A substitute solution doesn't solve the exact same problem at all, but satisfies enough of the same underlying need that a customer might choose it anyway — a dog-washing self-service station at the local pet store, which doesn't groom the dog but does address the "my dog needs attention" feeling behind the request.

Before exploring the full spectrum interactively, notice that these four categories — do-nothing, current workaround, indirect/substitute, and direct — form a rough line from "costs the customer nothing to keep choosing" to "looks almost exactly like your own offer." The map below lets you place Jordan's actual alternatives along that line.

docs.title: Diagram: Competitive Landscape Map
docs.text:
Competitive Landscape Map

Type: diagram sim-id: competitive-landscape-map Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4) Bloom Verb: differentiate

Learning objective: Learners differentiate existing alternatives to a venture as the do-nothing alternative, a current workaround, an indirect competitor or substitute, or a direct competitor, by their directness in solving the same problem.

Canvas layout:

  • A horizontal spectrum line labeled "How directly does this solve the same problem?" running from "Costs nothing to keep choosing" (left) to "Looks just like your offer" (right)
  • 5 nodes placed along the line, left to right: "Do-Nothing Alternative," "Current Workaround," "Substitute Solution," "Indirect Competitor," "Direct Competitor"
  • A detail panel below showing the selected node's definition and Jordan's real example

Data Visibility Requirements:

Do-Nothing Alternative selected: "Tolerating the problem unsolved. Jordan's example: the dog just doesn't get groomed this month." Current Workaround selected: "An informal, imperfect fix. Jordan's example: dry shampoo and at-home brushing." Substitute Solution selected: "Solves the underlying need differently. Jordan's example: a self-service dog wash station at the pet store." Indirect Competitor selected: "Solves the same problem, different approach. Jordan's example: a traditional storefront groomer requiring drop-off." Direct Competitor selected: "Same problem, same approach. Jordan's example: another mobile dog-grooming service in the area."

Interactive controls:

  • Click any node to select it and update the detail panel (default: no node selected, prompt reads "Click a node to explore Jordan's competitive landscape")
  • Selected node highlighted in fox-orange (#E8791A); others in indigo (#3F51B5)

Visual style: Simple horizontal spectrum line with 5 evenly spaced circular nodes; labels above each node, connecting line beneath.

Default parameters: No node selected on load.

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Store the 5 nodes as an array of objects {label, definition, example} with fixed x-positions along the spectrum. Must reflow to a vertical spectrum (top to bottom) on narrow (mobile) viewports.

docs.title: Researching the Landscape
docs.text:
Filling in the map above requires actual work, and the course uses several related terms for that work. Competitive research is the general activity of gathering information about existing alternatives available to your target customer. Competitive intelligence refers more specifically to the ongoing, ordered collection and interpretation of that information — not a one-time search, but a ledger a founder keeps updating. Competitive analysis is the step of interpreting gathered research to draw conclusions about strengths, weaknesses, and openings. The competitive landscape is the resulting full picture — every alternative a target customer has available, organized and understood together — and competitive landscape mapping is the specific act of laying that picture out visually, such as the spectrum diagram above.

Ask What They'd Do If You Didn't Exist

Here's a shortcut for competitive research: during a discovery interview, ask directly, "What would you do about this if my business didn't exist?" The answer names your real competitive landscape faster than any amount of online searching — straight from the customer who has to live with the choice.

docs.title: Finding the Gap
docs.text:
The entire point of mapping alternatives is spotting where they fall short. A market gap is a genuine, customer-confirmed shortfall shared by every current alternative — something the status quo consistently fails to deliver that a target customer actually wants. Alternative assessment is the deliberate evaluation of each mapped alternative against the validated problem from Chapter 5, checking specifically where it satisfies the customer and where it leaves them still wanting something more.

No Visible Competitors Is a Warning Sign, Not Good News

A common trap here is celebrating an empty competitive landscape as proof of a great opportunity. Usually it means one of two things: either the problem isn't real enough for anyone to have built a solution, or the research simply wasn't thorough. The fix: if your map looks empty, assume you're missing alternatives — especially the do-nothing kind — before assuming you've found a gap no one else has noticed.

docs.title: Differentiation and Positioning
docs.text: With a real market gap identified, two final ideas point forward to Chapter 8. Differentiation is what makes your offer meaningfully different from every mapped alternative, grounded in the specific gap you found rather than a vague claim of being "better." Competitive positioning is the deliberate choice of where your offer sits relative to the full competitive landscape in a customer's mind — faster, cheaper, more personal, more convenient — set up here and built out fully into a complete value proposition in the next chapter.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Before Chapter 8 turns this landscape into a value proposition, hold onto how the competitive picture comes together:

  • An alternative solution includes every existing solution that makes up the customer's status quo — starting with the often-overlooked do-nothing alternative and current workaround.
  • A true competitor can be direct, indirect, or a substitute solution — three different distances from your own offer along the same spectrum.
  • Competitive research, competitive intelligence, and competitive analysis build the full competitive landscape, laid out visually through competitive landscape mapping.
  • A genuine market gap, confirmed through honest alternative assessment, is what earns real differentiation and a clear competitive positioning — never assumed from an empty-looking map.

You Just Mapped the Real Competition

You now know exactly what your offer is up against — including the "nothing" that so many founders miss. That's the honest foundation Chapter 8 needs to build a value proposition on. Let's find out for real, starting with benefit and advantage in Chapter 8.

docs.title: Quiz: Alternatives & the Competitive Landscape
docs.text: Test your understanding of mapping alternatives and the competitive landscape with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How does the chapter define an alternative solution?
docs.text:
1. Anything a target customer currently uses, does, or chooses instead of your proposed offer to address their problem
  2. Any business that has raised more funding than your own venture
  3. A solution a founder plans to build after the current offer succeeds
  4. The single most expensive option available to a target customer
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An alternative solution is anything a target customer currently uses, does, or chooses instead of your proposed offer to address their problem — a category far broader than "other companies selling something similar." This broader definition is why the chapter warns founders against filling in the Alternatives block too narrowly, since the word "competitor" tempts people to think only of rival businesses.

Concept Tested: Alternative Solution

docs.title: 2. What counts as a competitor, according to the chapter's definition?
docs.text:
1. Only another registered business selling a product similar to your own
  2. Any government regulation that makes a venture harder to launch
  3. Any existing solution — business, product, or workaround — that a target customer might choose over your offer
  4. A customer who has expressed doubt about whether your offer will work
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A competitor is any existing solution — business, product, or workaround — that a target customer might choose over your offer. This definition deliberately extends beyond formal rival businesses to include informal workarounds and even the option of doing nothing, all of which a target customer might pick instead of the founder's offer.

Concept Tested: Competitor

docs.title: 3. How does the competitive landscape differ from a single competitor, as the chapter uses the terms?
docs.text:
1. The competitive landscape refers only to competitors located within the founder's own geographic area
  2. A competitor is one alternative a customer might choose; the competitive landscape is the full, organized picture of every alternative available to the target customer
  3. The two terms are synonyms and can be used interchangeably throughout the chapter
  4. The competitive landscape only includes direct competitors, while the term "competitor" includes all four categories
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A competitor is one specific alternative a customer might choose; the competitive landscape is the resulting full picture — every alternative a target customer has available, organized and understood together. Mapping individual competitors is a step toward building the broader competitive landscape, not the same thing as it.

Concept Tested: Competitive Landscape

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter classify Priya's interviewees' rotating mix of takeout, cereal for dinner, and a freezer of half-used ingredients as a current workaround rather than a competitor business?
docs.text:
1. Because it costs the customer money every single time it is used
  2. Because it was recommended to the customer by a dedicated meal-kit company
  3. Because it directly copies an existing storefront restaurant's approach
  4. Because it is an informal, imperfect method the customer assembled on their own to partially address the problem, without a dedicated solution
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A current workaround is any informal, imperfect method a customer has assembled on their own to partially address the problem without a dedicated solution. Priya's interviewees' rotating mix of takeout, cereal for dinner, and half-used freezer ingredients was exactly this kind of self-assembled, imperfect fix — not a competing meal-kit company.

Concept Tested: Current Workaround
