docs.title: Learning Graph for The Eight-Hour Entrepreneur
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement

Vew the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 4 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with 14 categories
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (5.3% - 9.3% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-6 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file

View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: The 300 concepts in the learning graph are organized into 14 categories, each evenly distributed (no category exceeds 10% of the total) and mapped to the course's week-by-week structure and the CO.STARTERS Canvas framework.

docs.title: FOUND — Entrepreneurship Foundations & Philosophy
docs.text: The mindset, vocabulary, and course philosophy underlying the whole program: what an early-stage venture is, the idea trap, the Clarity → Validation → Action → Launch philosophy, and the psychological-safety norms of the cohort.

docs.title: CANV — CO.STARTERS Canvas Framework
docs.text: The Business Model Canvas adaptation used throughout the course and its 11 individual blocks (Customer, Problem, Solution, Alternatives, Benefit, Advantage, Message, Distribution, Revenue, Startup Needs, Costs).

docs.title: CUST — Customer Discovery & Segmentation
docs.text: Identifying and defining who the venture serves: target customer, personas, market segments, and customer prioritization.

docs.title: PROB — Problem Definition & Pain Points
docs.text: Defining the real problem a customer has: pain points, root causes, problem severity/frequency, and problem validation.

docs.title: SOL — Solution Design & Offer Development
docs.text: Framing what is offered to solve the validated problem: initial offer, minimum viable offer, and solution iteration.

docs.title: ALT — Alternatives & Competitive Analysis
docs.text: How customers currently solve the problem: competitors, workarounds, substitutes, and competitive positioning.

docs.title: VALU — Value Proposition: Benefit & Advantage
docs.text: Why the customer wants the solution and why this founder is positioned to deliver it: benefit, advantage, and value-proposition articulation.

docs.title: INTV — Discovery Interviews & Research Methods
docs.text: Techniques for talking to real customers: interview design, the Reality Check pressure test, and synthesizing findings.

docs.title: VALID — Lean Validation & Testing
docs.text: Testing assumptions cheaply before building: lean tests, pre-selling, manual service delivery, and kill/pivot/persevere decisions.

docs.title: MSG — Messaging & Communication
docs.text: Turning a validated concept into clear, compelling communication: value-proposition statements, sales copy, and founder narrative.

docs.title: DIST — Distribution & Go-to-Market
docs.text: How the product or service reaches the customer: channel selection, word of mouth, and multi-channel strategy.

docs.title: REV — Revenue Models & Pricing
docs.text: How the venture makes money: pricing models, pricing validation, and willingness to pay.

docs.title: FIN — Startup Needs & Cost Planning
docs.text: One-time startup needs versus ongoing costs, and basic financial-planning literacy for a lean venture.

docs.title: LAUNCH — Launch Planning, Pitching & Accountability
docs.text: Synthesizing the canvas into a 30-day launch roadmap, pitching to peers, and the accountability structures that sustain momentum after the course.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
Only one element scored below full points:

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
The course description is well-suited to generating 200+ concepts:

  • 16 main topics, each mapping to a CO.STARTERS Canvas block or a discrete workshop activity (interviews, pressure test, lean testing, messaging, pricing, launch planning) — each topic alone can reasonably decompose into 8–15 concepts (definitions, techniques, examples, common pitfalls), suggesting 150–200+ concepts from topics alone.
  • 24 Bloom's-Taxonomy outcomes spanning all six levels, each implying distinct procedural or conceptual concepts (e.g., "pressure test," "lean validation test," "minimum testable iteration," "value proposition," "Startup Needs vs. Costs") that expand the topic-derived concept pool further.
  • The explicit Topics Not Covered section keeps scope bounded, which will help the learning-graph-generator avoid concept drift into adjacent domains (e.g., accounting, fundraising) that aren't part of this course.

Estimate: sufficient depth and breadth to reach the ~200-concept target without artificial padding.

docs.title: List of MicroSims for The Eight-Hour Entrepreneur
docs.text:
Interactive MicroSims that let you practice each step of the course: sorting assumptions from evidence, narrowing a customer, testing an offer, checking the numbers, and pitching.

  • 30-Day Launch Roadmap Timeline

    A step-through timeline of Jordan's 30-day launch plan showing each week's plan, weekly milestone, and weekly target, and how the four weeks build toward launch readiness.

  • Assumption Ledger Sorter

    A six-card sorting quiz in which learners classify statements from Jordan's dog-grooming idea as either untested assumptions or validated learning, with immediate feedback on every card.

  • Benefit vs Advantage Sorter

    A six-card sorting quiz in which learners classify value-proposition statements from Jordan's dog-grooming idea as customer Benefits or founder Advantages, with immediate feedback on every card.

  • Break-Even Calculator

    Learners adjust price, cost per sale, and fixed monthly cost sliders to calculate how many sales a lean venture needs to break even, starting from Jordan's $40 dog-grooming session.

  • CO.STARTERS Canvas Explorer

    A clickable map of the 11-block CO.STARTERS Canvas, filled in with Jordan's Session 1 dog-grooming answers, showing each block's guiding question, definition, example answer, and chapter.

  • Cohort Safety Signal Sorter

    A six-card sorting quiz in which learners classify moments from a live cohort session as Safety-Building or Safety-Eroding, with immediate feedback on every card.

  • Competitive Landscape Map

    Learners differentiate the five kinds of alternative to Jordan's mobile dog-grooming idea, from the do-nothing alternative to a direct competitor, by how directly each solves the same problem.

  • Customer Definition Funnel

    A step-through funnel that narrows Priya's meal-prep market from families who eat dinner down to Dana, one persona, showing each stage's definition, the filter that narrowed it, and a concrete example.

  • Distribution Channel Map

    An interactive scatter plot that places eight distribution channels by cost and reach, so learners can compare them and judge which ones fit an early-stage venture with limited resources.

  • Leading vs Open-Ended Question Sorter

    A six-card sorting quiz in which learners classify discovery-interview questions as open-ended or leading, with immediate feedback and an open-ended rewrite of every leading question.

  • Minimum Testable Iteration Decision Tree

    Learners judge whether service before product, manual before automated, and pre-selling before building apply to Jordan's or Priya's venture, then justify the minimum testable iteration the three judgments produce.

  • Minimum Viable Offer Slider

    Learners drag an Offer Scope slider to shrink or grow Jordan's mobile dog-grooming offer and see which features are the essential core and which are removable add-ons.

  • One-Sentence Value Proposition Builder

    Learners compose a one-sentence value proposition from four parts: target customer, core benefit, founder advantage, and main alternative. The sentence updates live, with feedback on missing parts, generic words, and read time.

  • Persevere vs Pivot Signal Checker

    Learners set three validation evidence signals to see whether the pattern supports a persevere, pivot, or kill decision, then judge the evidence from four practice ventures and get feedback on each signal.

  • Startup Needs Sorter

    A six-card sorting quiz in which learners classify items Jordan is considering buying as a Genuine Need or a want that can wait, with immediate feedback on every card.

  • Symptom vs Root Cause Drill-Down

    Learners apply the repeated why technique to Priya's first interview complaint, choosing the answer that explains each layer until they reach the root cause, with feedback on every dead end.

  • The Field Discovery Window Rhythm

    A step-through timeline of the four-week course showing what happens in each 2-hour live session and each 7-day Field Discovery Window, and how each one feeds the next.

  • The Four-Phase Founder Pipeline

    A step-through infographic of the Clarity, Validation, Action, and Launch phases, pairing each definition with Jordan's concrete example and a predict-before-you-advance prompt.

  • The Idea Trap Cycle

    An interactive diagram that contrasts the closed "refine the plan" loop with the open "real-world test" path, using counters to show that only testing produces real customer answers.

  • Two-Minute Pitch Structure and Timer

    Learners study the four timed sections of Jordan's two-minute pitch (Problem, Solution, Evidence, Ask), then rehearse their own pitch against a 120-second countdown that highlights each section on time.

docs.title: Assumption Ledger Sorter
docs.text: Run the Assumption Ledger Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every business idea starts out built entirely from assumptions. The skill this MicroSim practices is telling the difference between a statement someone has actually tested and one that only sounds true.

Learners work through six cards from Jordan's ledger, the running list of beliefs and findings behind Jordan's mobile dog-grooming idea. For each card they choose Assumption or Validated Learning. The feedback is immediate:

  • A correct answer flashes green; an incorrect answer flashes amber.
  • The correct category is stamped on the card.
  • A one-sentence explanation says why, so a wrong answer still teaches something.

Some cards are deliberately tricky. "2 of 5 neighbors said the price was too high" is validated learning even though it is bad news, and "A mobile service is obviously more convenient" is an assumption even though it sounds reasonable.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the statement on the card.
  2. Click Assumption or Validated Learning.
  3. Read the feedback, then click Next Card.
  4. After card 6, click See Results for your score and a review of any cards you missed.
  5. Click Try Again to sort the same six cards in a new, shuffled order.

The progress bar across the top turns green or amber for each card as you go. Nothing is saved; the score lasts only for the current session.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Given short statements from Jordan's dog-grooming-van idea, participants will classify each one as an Assumption (untested) or Validated Learning (tested), applying the chapter's definitions to concrete cases.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3). Bloom Verb: classify.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 1 reading on assumptions and validated learning

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Solo sort (4 min): Each participant sorts all six cards and notes their score.
  2. Debrief the tricky cards (3 min): As a group, discuss cards 4 and 5. Why is bad news still validated learning? Why does "obviously" signal an untested belief?
  3. Sort your own ledger (3 min): Each participant writes three statements about their own idea and labels each one, asking "how do I know this?" for every line.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Did the participant classify at least 5 of 6 cards correctly on a second attempt?
  • Can the participant explain why a customer's "no" counts as validated learning?
  • Can the participant rewrite one of their own assumptions as a test they could run this week?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Lean startup - Wikipedia - Defines validated learning, the category that real customer evidence falls into.
  2. Hypothesis - Wikipedia - An assumption is a business hypothesis that has not been tested yet.
  3. Confirmation bias - Wikipedia - Why statements that "sound obviously true" are easy to mistake for evidence.
  4. The Mom Test - Rob Fitzpatrick - How to gather customer feedback that counts as real evidence instead of polite opinion.

docs.title: Benefit vs Advantage Sorter
docs.text: Run the Benefit vs Advantage Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A value proposition answers two separate questions: why the customer wants the solution (the Benefit) and why this founder is the one to deliver it (the Advantage). Most weak pitches answer only one of them, and founders often mix the two up in their own writing.

Learners work through six statements from Jordan's mobile dog-grooming pitch and choose Benefit or Advantage for each. The feedback is immediate:

  • A correct answer flashes green; an incorrect answer flashes amber.
  • The correct category is stamped on the card.
  • A one-sentence explanation says why, so a wrong answer still teaches something.

Two cards are deliberately tricky. "Affordable, convenient grooming that comes to you" sounds like a claim about the business, but it describes value the customer receives, so it is a benefit. "I can respond same-day" helps the customer, but it rests on a fact about the founder (Jordan lives in the neighborhood), so it is an advantage.

  2. Click Benefit or Advantage.
  3. Read the feedback, then click Next Card.

  5. Click Try Again to sort the same six cards in a new, shuffled order.

The progress bar across the top turns green or amber for each card as you go. The stack behind the current card shrinks as cards are dealt. Nothing is saved; the score lasts only for the current session.

docs.title: Break-Even Calculator
docs.text: Run the Break-Even Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Break-even is the number of sales at which a month's revenue exactly covers the month's costs. Three numbers decide it:

  • Price per Sale: what one customer pays
  • Cost per Sale: what it costs to deliver that one sale
  • Fixed Monthly Costs: what the venture pays each month no matter how much it sells

Each sale leaves Price minus Cost toward the fixed costs. Dividing the fixed costs by that amount gives the break-even point:

Sales needed = Fixed Monthly Costs ÷ (Price per Sale − Cost per Sale)

Nobody can make three quarters of a sale, so the answer always rounds up to the next whole sale. The sliders start at Jordan's numbers from the chapter: a $40 driveway session, $8 cost per sale, and $120 in fixed monthly costs.

Step Jordan's numbers Each sale leaves $40 − $8 = $32 Fixed costs ÷ per-sale amount $120 ÷ $32 = 3.75 Round up to a whole sale 4 sales Check 4 × $32 = $128, which covers the $120

The result card shows this division with whatever numbers the sliders hold. Below it, a bar shows Sales This Month on a 0-30 scale against an indigo break-even line. The bar is red below the line and green at or above it, and the line under the bar works out the month's profit or loss.

If the price is at or below the cost per sale, each sale leaves nothing (or less than nothing) toward the fixed costs, so no number of sales can break even. The card replaces the answer with a warning instead of dividing by zero or a negative number.

On a phone-width screen the formula is written with numbers only and the hint beside the button is hidden.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the result card. With Jordan's numbers, 4 sales are needed to break even.
  2. The bar starts at 0 sales, in red. Drag Sales This Month to 3, then 4, and watch the bar turn green at the break-even line.
  3. Change one number at a time. Raise Price per Sale, then lower it; raise Cost per Sale; raise Fixed Monthly Costs. Before each move, predict whether the number of sales needed will go up or down.
  4. Drag Cost per Sale above Price per Sale to see the warning.
  5. Click Load Jordan's Numbers to return to $40, $8 and $120, with 5 sales this month.
  6. After you click a slider, the left and right arrow keys move it one step at a time.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will calculate how many sales a lean venture needs to break even in a month by adjusting price, cost per sale, and fixed monthly costs, and explain why the answer rounds up to a whole sale.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3). Bloom Verb: calculate.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 14 reading through "Projecting Revenue and Finding Break-Even"
  • Basic arithmetic: subtraction, division, and rounding

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Check Jordan's number (3 min): Before anyone touches a slider, participants work out \(120 ÷ (\)40 − $8) by hand and type their answer in the chat. The facilitator then shares the screen and compares the answer with the result card, including why 3.75 becomes 4.
  2. Predict, then move (5 min): The facilitator calls out a change, such as "Cost per Sale goes to $16" or "Fixed Monthly Costs doubles to $240." Participants predict the new break-even number in the chat before the slider moves, then compare.
  3. Find the danger zone (2 min): Each participant drags Cost per Sale up until the warning appears and explains in one sentence why no number of sales can fix it.
  4. Run your own numbers (5 min): Each participant enters a price, cost per sale, and fixed monthly costs for their own venture idea, records the break-even number, and decides whether that many sales a month is realistic given their lean test results.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Given a price, cost per sale, and fixed monthly costs, can the participant calculate the break-even number by hand, including rounding up?
  • Can the participant explain why a break-even of 3.75 means 4 sales, not 3?
  • Can the participant predict which way the break-even number moves when each input rises or falls?
  • Can the participant explain why a price at or below the cost per sale can never break even?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Break-even (economics) - Wikipedia - The point at which total revenue equals total cost, and the formula this calculator uses.
  2. Contribution margin - Wikipedia - The amount each sale leaves toward fixed costs after its own cost is paid, the Price minus Cost in the formula.
  3. Fixed cost - Wikipedia - Costs that stay the same regardless of how much a business sells, the bar break-even has to clear.
  4. Variable cost - Wikipedia - Costs that rise and fall with each sale, the Cost per Sale slider.
  5. Cost-volume-profit analysis - Wikipedia - The wider method of seeing how price, costs, and sales volume together decide profit.

docs.title: Cohort Safety Signal Sorter
docs.text: Run the Cohort Safety Signal Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Psychological safety is a shared belief that a group is safe for interpersonal risk-taking: no one will be embarrassed, rejected, or penalized for speaking up, admitting a mistake, or asking a question. The signal for it is rarely in what someone discloses. It is in how the room responds.

Learners work through six cards, each describing something said or done during a cohort session, and choose Safety-Building or Safety-Eroding. The feedback is immediate:

  • A correct answer flashes green; an incorrect answer flashes amber.
  • The correct category is stamped on the card.
  • A one-sentence explanation says why, so a wrong answer still teaches something.

Two cards are deliberately tricky. The participant who goes quiet after being mocked is not doing anything wrong; the silence is the visible cost of an earlier unsafe moment. The founder who polishes a canvas overnight hears no criticism at all, yet fear of judgment is already changing what the group gets to see.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the cohort moment on the card.
  2. Click Safety-Building or Safety-Eroding.
  3. Read the feedback, then click Next Card.
  4. After card 6, click See Results for your score and a review of all six moments.
  5. Click Try Again to sort the same six cards in a new, shuffled order.

The progress bar across the top turns green or amber for each card as you go. The stack behind the current card shrinks as cards are dealt. Nothing is saved; the score lasts only for the current session.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Given short statements describing things said or done during a cohort session, participants will classify each one as Safety-Building or Safety-Eroding, applying the chapter's definition of psychological safety to concrete cohort moments.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3). Bloom Verb: classify.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 2 reading on psychological safety, including Priya's Session 2 check-in

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Solo sort (4 min): Each participant sorts all six cards and notes their score.
  2. Debrief the quiet signals (3 min): As a group, discuss cards 4 and 6. Nobody in either card says anything harsh. What tells you safety is eroding anyway?
  3. Name your room's norm (3 min): Each participant writes one sentence the group could say or do in the next breakout room that would make an honest "my test flopped" easier to share.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Did the participant classify at least 5 of 6 cards correctly on a second, shuffled attempt?
  • Can the participant explain why a silent participant can be a sign of eroded safety?
  • Can the participant rewrite a Safety-Eroding moment as a Safety-Building response, such as replacing unsolicited advice with a clarifying question?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Psychological safety - Wikipedia - The definition this sorter applies, including Amy Edmondson's research on team learning.
  2. Amy Edmondson - Wikipedia - The Harvard researcher who defined team psychological safety and wrote The Fearless Organization.
  3. Peer learning - Wikipedia - How learners teach each other, and why a peer's response shapes what the next person is willing to share.
  4. Community of practice - Wikipedia - Background on peer groups that learn together, the model behind a cohort's peer learning community.

docs.title: Competitive Landscape Map
docs.text: Run the Competitive Landscape Map MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Ask a first-time founder about competitors and they usually list businesses that sell something like their own offer. This map widens the view to everything Jordan's target customer could choose instead of a mobile dog groomer, and it sorts those alternatives by one question: how directly does this solve the same problem?

The five alternatives sit along a spectrum. The left end is the option that costs the customer nothing to keep choosing. The right end is the option that looks just like Jordan's offer. Each step to the right adds exactly one thing, labeled under the line:

# Alternative Jordan's example What this step adds 1 Do-Nothing Alternative The dog just doesn't get groomed this month Starting point 2 Current Workaround Dry shampoo and at-home brushing A fix 3 Substitute Solution A self-service dog wash station at the pet store A dedicated offer 4 Indirect Competitor A traditional storefront groomer requiring drop-off The same problem 5 Direct Competitor Another mobile dog-grooming service in the area The same approach

Clicking a node turns it fox orange and fills the detail panel with four things:

  • The definition of that kind of alternative.
  • Jordan's example of it.
  • Why it sits here: the step it has taken and the one it has not.
  • Where it falls short for Jordan's customer.

The "falls short" lines are the raw material for a market gap. The indirect competitor, for example, falls short on exactly the problem Jordan validated in Chapter 5: a half-day lost to drop-off and pickup.

On a phone-width screen the spectrum turns vertical, running from top (least direct) to bottom (most direct), with the step labels on the right.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question above the spectrum and the two end labels.
  2. Click any node, or its label, to open its details in the panel below.
  3. Click More direct → or ← Less direct to step to the neighboring node. The left and right arrow keys do the same once the MicroSim has focus.
  4. Compare two neighbors: which single difference separates them?
  5. Click Clear to return to the opening prompt.

The status line next to Clear counts how many of the five alternatives you have explored.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Learners differentiate existing alternatives to a venture as the do-nothing alternative, a current workaround, an indirect competitor or substitute, or a direct competitor, by their directness in solving the same problem.

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4). Bloom Verb: differentiate.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 5 reading on Jordan's problem definition: the half-day lost to an in-person drop-off and pickup
  • Chapter 7 reading through "Direct, Indirect, and Substitute Competitors"

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Walk the spectrum (4 min): Each participant clicks all five nodes from left to right and notes what each step adds.
  2. Name the boundary (4 min): In breakout pairs, pick two neighboring nodes and state the one difference between them. Then discuss the hardest boundary on the map: the self-service wash station and the storefront groomer are both dedicated businesses, so why is only one of them an indirect competitor?
  3. Map your own idea (5 min): Each participant lists one alternative of each kind for their own venture, starting from the question "What would you do about this if my business didn't exist?" Any empty slot, especially the do-nothing slot, is a sign the research is not finished yet.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Given an alternative that is not on the map, can the participant place it on the spectrum and name the step it has not taken?
  • Can the participant explain why the do-nothing alternative is often the toughest competitor, even though it costs the customer nothing?
  • Can the participant name one shortfall shared by every alternative on their own map, as a first candidate for a market gap?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Competitor analysis - Wikipedia - How businesses identify and assess direct and indirect competitors.
  2. Substitute good - Wikipedia - The economics behind substitutes: different products that meet the same underlying need.
  3. Porter's five forces analysis - Wikipedia - Places the threat of substitutes alongside rivalry among direct competitors.
  4. Status quo bias - Wikipedia - Why customers keep choosing to do nothing even when a better option exists.
  5. Obviously Awesome by April Dunford (2019) - A positioning method that starts from a product's competitive alternatives, including doing nothing, rather than from rival companies alone.

docs.title: CO.STARTERS Canvas Explorer
docs.text: Run the CO.STARTERS Canvas Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The CO.STARTERS Canvas is one page with 11 blocks, and each block answers one plain-language question about a venture. This MicroSim lays the blocks out in the same four rows as the canvas sheet:

  • Customer and Problem across the top
  • Solution, Alternatives, Benefit, and Advantage in the second row
  • Message, Distribution, and Revenue in the third row
  • Startup Needs and Costs along the bottom

Click any block and the panel below the grid shows four things:

  1. The guiding question the block answers
  2. A one-sentence definition of the block
  3. Jordan's answer from the Session 1 draft of the mobile dog-grooming canvas
  4. The later chapter that covers the block in depth

Show All Answers writes Jordan's short answer inside every block, so the whole worked example can be read as one page. None of Jordan's answers runs longer than a sentence, which is the index-card size limit working as intended. Reading across the filled-in grid is also a first taste of canvas synthesis: the Customer, Distribution, and Message answers should all point at the same group of people.

On a phone-width screen the grid reflows into a single column in canvas order, and the answers appear beside each block label.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any block to select it. The block gets a fox-orange outline and the panel fills in.
  2. Click Next and Previous to step through all 11 blocks in canvas order. The left and right arrow keys do the same thing.
  3. Click Show All Answers to see Jordan's answer inside every block. Click Hide All Answers to return to the blank canvas.
  4. A check mark appears on each block you have explored. The counter at the bottom right turns green when all 11 have been explored.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will explain the guiding question each of the 11 CO.STARTERS Canvas blocks answers, and locate Jordan's example answer for each block, by clicking through the full canvas layout.

Bloom Level: Understand (L2). Bloom Verb: explain.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1 reading on early-stage ventures and the idea trap
  • Chapter 3 reading through the "Jordan's Canvas So Far" table

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Guided walk (4 min): The facilitator shares the screen and clicks Next through all 11 blocks. Participants say each guiding question out loud before the panel shows it.
  2. Pair explain (5 min): In breakout pairs, one partner names a block and the other explains its guiding question in their own words, then checks the panel. Swap after five blocks.
  3. Read across the page (4 min): Turn on Show All Answers. Each participant reads Jordan's Customer, Distribution, and Message answers together and says whether they point at the same people.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant state the guiding question for any block without clicking it?
  • Can the participant explain the difference between the Benefit block and the Advantage block?
  • Can the participant explain the difference between the Startup Needs block and the Costs block, using one of Jordan's answers as an example?
  • Given one of Jordan's answers read aloud, can the participant name the block it belongs to?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Business Model Canvas - Wikipedia - The nine-block strategic-planning tool that the CO.STARTERS Canvas simplifies for ventures that have not started yet.
  2. CO.STARTERS - CO.STARTERS - The organization behind the canvas and the cohort program this course is built around.
  3. Lean startup - Wikipedia - Why each block is a first draft to test rather than a final answer to defend.
  4. Value proposition - Wikipedia - Background for the Benefit and Advantage blocks, which together make up a value proposition.

docs.title: Customer Definition Funnel
docs.text: Run the Customer Definition Funnel MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A customer definition gets precise one cut at a time. This MicroSim draws that narrowing as a funnel of five bands, widest at the top:

  1. Broad Market
  2. Market Segment
  3. Niche Market
  4. Target Customer
  5. Ideal Customer Profile / Persona

The worked example is Priya's meal-prep idea from Chapter 4. Her market starts as "Families who eat dinner" and ends as Dana, a 34-year-old ER nurse on rotating 12-hour shifts who values ten minutes saved more than variety. Each band in between adds one filter: income and household structure, then a shared daily pain, then shift work and Priya's delivery area.

The selected band turns fox-orange, and the detail panel shows:

  • A one-sentence definition of the stage
  • Narrowed by: the filter that took the group from the band above to this one
  • Priya's example: her actual description of the customer at this stage
  • One band wider: the example from the stage above, for a side-by-side comparison (shown when the screen has room)

The bottom band combines two tools from the chapter. The ideal customer profile lists the traits of a best-fit customer, and the persona turns those traits into one named person. Dana is both.

On a phone-width screen the funnel reflows into a shallow stack of labeled bands with the detail panel below it.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. The funnel opens with Broad Market selected. Read the panel before moving on.
  2. Click Narrow Next to move one band down the funnel. Click Widen Back to move one band up. The arrow keys do the same thing: down or right narrows, up or left widens.
  3. Click any band to jump straight to that stage.
  4. At each stage, compare Priya's example with the band one level wider and find the words that were added. Those words are the filter named in the Narrowed by line.
  5. The counter at the bottom right turns green when all five stages have been explored.

        height="542px"

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will explain how a broad market narrows step by step into a target customer, an ideal customer profile, and a persona, and locate Priya's concrete example at each stage, by stepping through the funnel one band at a time.

Bloom Level: Understand (L2). Bloom Verb: explain.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 3 reading on the Customer block of the CO.STARTERS Canvas
  • Chapter 4 reading through "From Broad Market to Target Customer"

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict the cut (4 min): The facilitator shares the screen with Broad Market selected. Before each click of Narrow Next, participants type in the chat the filter they expect Priya to add, then compare with the Narrowed by line.
  2. Pair explain (5 min): In breakout pairs, one partner names a band and the other explains what makes it narrower than the band above, using Priya's example as evidence. Swap after two bands.
  3. Map Jordan's funnel (4 min): Each participant places Jordan's three stages from the chapter ("dog owners," "dog owners without easy access to a groomer," and "dog owners within 5 miles who've expressed frustration with driving to get their dog groomed") on the matching bands and says which filter separates each one from the next.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Given one of Priya's five examples read aloud out of order, can the participant name its stage?
  • Can the participant explain what separates a niche market from a market segment?
  • Can the participant explain why "Families who eat dinner" is not yet a target customer?
  • Can the participant explain the difference between a target customer (a group) and a persona (one named person)?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Market segmentation - Wikipedia - The bases (demographic, behavioral, geographic) used to split a broad market into segments.
  2. Niche market - Wikipedia - Why a small, well-defined segment can be served better by a small venture than by a large one.
  3. Target market - Wikipedia - How a venture chooses the group it will serve first and aims its offer at them.
  4. Total addressable market - Wikipedia - The total, serviceable, and obtainable market distinction behind Priya's "within her metro delivery area" filter.
  5. Persona (user experience) - Wikipedia - Research-grounded composite characters like Dana, used to make design decisions for one realistic person.

docs.title: Distribution Channel Map
docs.text: Run the Distribution Channel Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every distribution channel trades channel cost (the money, time, or both it takes to use) against channel reach (how many target customers it can realistically expose your offer to). This scatter plot puts the eight channels from Chapter 13 on one map so you can compare them directly instead of reading a list:

  • The three broad shapes: Direct Sales, Online Distribution, and In-Person Distribution.
  • The five specific types: Word of Mouth, Referral, Partnership, Marketplace, and Social Media.

Cost runs left to right and reach runs bottom to top, each on a relative 1-10 scale. The shaded green zone in the lower left holds the channels that fit an early-stage, low-capital venture: a cost of 4 or less, with narrow to moderate reach. Six channels sit inside it. Online Distribution and Marketplace sit outside, because their wider reach comes with platform fees, ads, or build costs.

The ratings are relative judgments for a typical early-stage local venture like Jordan's mobile dog-grooming service, not measurements. Selecting a channel fills the detail panel with concrete facts:

  • Cost and Reach: the rating and the reason for it.
  • What it is: the chapter's one-sentence definition.
  • Best for: the kind of venture the channel suits.
  • Wider reach for the same or less cost: any channel that beats this one on both axes of the chart.
  • Example: Jordan's or Priya's version of the channel.

The Compare with menu adds a second channel as an amber diamond, draws a dashed line between the two, and switches the panel to a side-by-side table with a verdict on the tradeoff. Direct Sales and In-Person Distribution share the same rating (3, 2), so their points are nudged slightly apart to keep both clickable. The tooltip and the panel always show the true values.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over any point to see the channel's definition and its cost and reach ratings.
  2. Click a point to select it. It turns fox orange and the detail panel shows its facts. On a phone, tap a point instead; the panel shows the same definition.
  3. Click Next and Previous (or press the arrow keys) to step through the channels from cheapest to most expensive.
  4. Choose a channel from Compare with to see the two side by side. Read the Tradeoff line: how much extra reach the costlier channel buys, or whether one channel beats the other on both cost and reach.
  5. Set Compare with back to (none) to return to the single-channel view.

On narrow screens the panel sits below the chart and drops the optional lines when space runs out. Wide screens show every line.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will compare distribution channels by their channel cost and channel reach, analyze the tradeoff between the two, and judge which channels best fit an early-stage venture with limited resources.

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4). Bloom Verb: compare.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 13 reading on distribution channels, channel cost, channel reach, and channel fit
  • Chapter 4's definition of the target customer
  • Jordan's mobile dog-grooming example from earlier chapters

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the map (3 min): Each participant steps through all eight channels with Next and notes which ones sit inside the best-fit zone and why the other two do not.
  2. Find the channels nothing beats (4 min): Using the "Wider reach for the same or less cost" line or the Compare with menu, find the channels that no other channel beats on both cost and reach. (Word of Mouth, Social Media, Online, and Marketplace.) As a group, discuss why Direct Sales is still a smart way to win the first customers even though four channels beat it on this chart.
  3. Compare pairs (4 min): In pairs, compare Word of Mouth with Marketplace and Referral with Social Media. Read each tradeoff verdict, then decide which channel Jordan should test first with a small budget, and what would have to be true about Jordan's customers to choose the other one.
  4. Apply it to your idea (4 min): Each participant picks two channels from the zone, names where their own target customer already pays attention, and chooses one channel to test this week.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant explain why Marketplace sits outside the best-fit zone even though it has the widest reach?
  • Given any two channels, can the participant state the difference in cost and reach and say which one suits a low-capital venture?
  • Can the participant describe a case where channel fit overrules the chart, such as a customer group that never uses the cheapest channel?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Distribution (marketing) - Wikipedia - How products and services reach customers, including direct and indirect channels.
  2. Word-of-mouth marketing - Wikipedia - Why satisfied customers telling others is both the cheapest and one of the most trusted channels.
  3. Referral marketing - Wikipedia - Turning word of mouth into a deliberate, rewarded system, the step from Word of Mouth to the Referral Channel.
  4. Online marketplace - Wikipedia - How third-party platforms trade fees and competition for built-in customer traffic.
  5. Pareto efficiency - Wikipedia - The idea behind "wider reach for the same or less cost": an option is dominated when another one is at least as good on every dimension and better on one.

docs.title: The Field Discovery Window Rhythm
docs.text: Run the Field Discovery Window Rhythm MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Eight-Hour Entrepreneur has two kinds of time. Four live sessions of two hours each happen inside the cohort, on video. Three Field Discovery Windows of seven days each happen outside it, where participants test their canvas blocks against real people. This timeline draws both to scale:

  • Each live session is a thin, solid indigo block in the top row, "Inside the cohort."
  • Each Field Discovery Window (FDW) is a wide, dashed fox-orange segment in the bottom row, "Out in the field."

The difference in width is the lesson. The course has 8 hours of live instruction and 21 days of field work, so most of the real work happens between sessions, not during them.

Selecting an entry opens a detail panel with three concrete pieces:

  • What happens: the assignment for that session or window.
  • Jordan's version: what Jordan does with it for the mobile dog-grooming idea.
  • How it connects: what the entry takes in from the one before it and hands to the one after it. Each session turns the last window's evidence into canvas blocks, and each window tests the blocks the last session produced.

On wide screens a course clock at the bottom of the panel adds up the live hours and field days completed so far.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start at Step 1: Session 1, which is selected when the page loads.
  2. Click Next to move one entry forward in course order, or Previous to go back. The left and right arrow keys work too.
  3. Click any block on the timeline to jump straight to it. Hover over a block for a one-line preview.
  4. For each entry, read How it connects and name what it received from the previous entry and what it passes on.

On a phone, the timeline keeps a readable width and scrolls sideways. Each step scrolls its entry into view.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will explain what happens during each live session and each Field Discovery Window across the four-week course, and describe the relationship between the two: live sessions turn evidence into canvas blocks, and Field Discovery Windows test those blocks with real customers.

Bloom Level: Understand (L2). Bloom Verb: explain.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 2 reading on the virtual learning lab, cohort-based learning, and the Field Discovery Window
  • Chapter 1's Jordan example (the mobile dog-grooming idea)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Step through the course (4 min): Each participant clicks Next through all seven entries and reads the three parts of each detail panel.
  2. Compare the widths (2 min): As a group, compare the width of one indigo session block with one orange window. Ask: where does most of the course's work actually happen, and why is it placed there instead of in the live sessions?
  3. Trace one handoff (4 min): In pairs, pick one window. One partner explains what it tested from the session before it; the other explains what the session after it builds from its results. Then each partner writes the FDW 1 task for their own idea in one sentence.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant state the assignment for any session or window without looking?
  • Can the participant explain why Session 2 cannot happen before FDW 1 finishes?
  • Can the participant describe the difference between a live session and a Field Discovery Window using the words "cohort" and "real customers"?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Customer development - Wikipedia - Steve Blank's method of leaving the building to test assumptions with customers, the idea behind every Field Discovery Window.
  2. Lean startup - Wikipedia - The build-measure-learn loop that the session-then-window rhythm repeats three times.
  3. Experiential learning - Wikipedia - Kolb's cycle of doing, reflecting, and applying, which the alternation of field work and live debrief follows.
  4. Spacing effect - Wikipedia - Why learning spread across weeks, with gaps between sessions, tends to last longer than the same hours packed into one block.
  5. The Mom Test - Rob Fitzpatrick - How to run the customer conversations that FDW 1 asks for without collecting polite, useless compliments.

docs.title: The Four-Phase Founder Pipeline
docs.text: Run the Four-Phase Founder Pipeline MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This course runs on a four-phase philosophy: Clarity → Validation → Action → Launch. The MicroSim lets participants step through the phases at their own pace instead of watching an animation they cannot pause. Each phase shows three things:

  • What it means: a one-sentence definition of the phase.
  • Jordan's example: what Jordan, the dog-grooming-van founder from Chapter 1, actually did in that phase.
  • Before you click Next: a question that asks the learner to predict the next move before seeing it.

A curved return arrow from Validation back to Clarity, labeled if evidence says pivot, shows that the phases form a cycle. Clicking Next on Launch loops back to Clarity for the same reason: every launch produces new evidence that sharpens the next round.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. The sim opens on Clarity. Read the definition and Jordan's example.
  2. Answer the Before you click Next question in your head (or in the chat), then click Next ▶.
  3. Click any phase box to jump straight to it. ◀ Previous steps back.
  4. Click the curved if evidence says pivot arrow to see why Validation can send you back to Clarity.
  5. On Launch, the Next button becomes Back to Clarity ↺ to show that the cycle repeats.

The left and right arrow keys also step through the phases once the sim has focus. On narrow screens the four boxes stack vertically.

Bloom Level: Understand (L2). Bloom Verb: explain.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

  • Familiarity with Jordan's mobile dog-grooming example

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Guided walk-through (5 min): The facilitator shares the sim and pauses on each phase. Before each click of Next, participants type their prediction into the chat.
  2. Pivot scenario (3 min): Click the return arrow. Ask: what evidence would send Jordan back to Clarity? What would change in Jordan's one-sentence guess?
  3. Apply to your own idea (5 min): In breakout rooms, each participant writes their own one-line example for Clarity and Validation, using Jordan's examples as a model.

docs.text:

  • Can the participant describe a piece of evidence that would trigger a pivot back to Clarity?

docs.title: The Idea Trap Cycle
docs.text: Run the Idea Trap Cycle MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The idea trap is hard to spot from the inside because it looks like diligence. This MicroSim puts the two ways a founder can spend the next hour side by side. On the left, Unrefined Business Idea and Refine the Plan form a closed loop: pitch decks, logos, and spreadsheets feel like progress, but the arrow always leads back to the same unanswered question. On the right, a straight path runs from the idea to a Real-World Test and ends at Validated Learning, a real answer of yes or no.

The example follows Jordan, the founder from Chapter 1 who wants to drive a dog-grooming van to customers' homes. Two counters make the contrast concrete: Hours invested climbs on both paths, but Real customer answers only moves when Jordan runs a real-world test.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any box to read what it means, with Jordan's version of it.
  2. Hover over (or tap) an arrow. The loop and the forward path each explain what kind of path they are.
  3. Click Refine the Plan several times. Watch Jordan circle the loop while hours pile up and customer answers stay at zero.
  4. Click Test with Customers. Jordan moves down the forward path, and each test adds real answers, including answers of "no."
  5. Click Reset to start over.

On narrow screens the loop sits on top and the forward path runs down the right side.

docs.text:
Participants will be able to differentiate productive early-stage activity (real-world testing) from unproductive activity (endless refinement) and recognize when they are personally in the idea trap.

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4). Bloom Verb: differentiate.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

  • An unrefined business idea of their own

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Individually, click all four boxes and hover both arrows.
  2. Predict and test (3 min): Before touching the buttons, predict how many times Jordan must click Refine the Plan before the customer-answers counter moves. Then try it, and compare with one click of Test with Customers.
  3. Breakout discussion (4 min): In breakout rooms, each person lists the last three things they did for their own idea and sorts each one onto the loop or the forward path.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant explain why refining a plan never changes the customer-answers count?
  • Can the participant name one "forward path" action they will take before the next session?
  • Does the participant recognize that a "no" from a real customer is still validated learning?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Lean startup - Wikipedia - Overview of the build-measure-learn approach and the idea of validated learning that the forward path represents.
  2. Customer development - Wikipedia - Steve Blank's method of getting out of the building to test assumptions with real customers.
  3. The Mom Test - Rob Fitzpatrick - A practical guide to asking customers questions that produce honest, useful answers.
  4. CO.STARTERS - The entrepreneurship program whose canvas and philosophy this course adapts.

docs.title: Leading vs Open-Ended Question Sorter
docs.text: Run the Leading vs Open-Ended Question Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
How a question is worded decides whether a discovery interview produces evidence or just polite agreement. An open-ended question asks the customer to supply the content in their own words. A leading question supplies the content itself and only asks the customer to agree.

Learners work through six cards, each a question Jordan might ask a dog owner about grooming, and choose Open-Ended or Leading. The feedback is immediate:

  • A correct answer flashes green; an incorrect answer flashes amber.
  • The correct category is stamped on the card.
  • A one-sentence explanation says why, so a wrong answer still teaches something.
  • Every leading question gets an open-ended rewrite on the card, showing how to ask the same thing without suggesting the answer.

Two cards are deliberately tricky. "Tell me about the last time getting your dog groomed was a hassle" mentions a problem, yet it is still open-ended because the customer tells the story. "This would save you so much time, right?" is a statement with "right?" added at the end, and that tag is what makes it leading.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the interview question on the card.
  2. Click Open-Ended or Leading.
  3. Read the feedback. For a leading question, read the open-ended rewrite on the card.
  4. Click Next Card. After card 6, click See Results for your score and a review of all six questions.
  5. Click Try Again to sort the same six cards in a new, shuffled order.

The progress bar across the top turns green or amber for each card as you go. The stack behind the current card shrinks as cards are dealt. Nothing is saved; the score lasts only for the current session.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Given sample discovery-interview questions, participants will classify each one as open-ended or leading, applying the chapter's unbiased interview design principles.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3). Bloom Verb: classify.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 9 reading on discovery interviews, especially the section on asking, not selling

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Solo sort (3 min): Each participant sorts all six cards and notes their score.
  2. Debrief the tricky cards (3 min): As a group, discuss the "hassle" card and the "right?" card. What makes the first one open-ended even though it names a problem? Why does adding "right?" turn a statement into a leading question?
  3. Rewrite your own script (4 min): Each participant writes three questions for their own discovery interviews, runs the stranger test on each one (could a stranger answer "no" without feeling awkward?), and rewrites any that fail as open-ended questions.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Did the participant classify at least 5 of 6 cards correctly on a second, shuffled attempt?
  • Can the participant explain the difference in terms of who supplies the content: the customer or the question?
  • Can the participant rewrite a leading question from their own script as an open-ended question about past behavior?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Leading question - Wikipedia - The definition this sorter applies: a question worded to suggest its own answer.
  2. Open-ended question - Wikipedia - Questions that cannot be answered with a simple yes or no.
  3. Customer development - Wikipedia - Steve Blank's method of getting out of the building to learn from real customers, the origin of the discovery interview.
  4. Response bias - Wikipedia - How question wording and politeness push answers away from what people actually think.
  5. The Mom Test - Rob Fitzpatrick - A short book on asking customers about their past behavior instead of fishing for compliments on your idea.

docs.title: Minimum Testable Iteration Decision Tree
docs.text: Run the Minimum Testable Iteration Decision Tree MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A minimum testable iteration is the smallest version of an offer that can get a real yes-or-no answer from a real customer. Three principles cut an idea down to that size: service before product, manual before automated, and pre-selling before building. This MicroSim asks you to judge whether each one applies to a specific venture.

The tree has three yes/no decision diamonds, one per principle. At each diamond you choose between two answers, and each answer comes with its reasoning:

  • One answer holds. Its reasoning fits the venture, such as "Jordan can groom one dog in a customer's driveway this week." The Yes branch turns green, the design note for that principle fills in beneath the diamond, and the next diamond opens.
  • The other is a common founder objection, such as "Mobile grooming can't start until the van is bought and fitted out." The No branch turns amber and shows a Reconsider note. The feedback explains why the objection doesn't hold for this venture, and you decide again.

After the third diamond, the card shows the combined design. For Jordan it is a manually booked, pre-paid, single driveway grooming session, with no van, no app and no inventory. The tree keeps the whole path visible, including every Reconsider branch you took, so each part of the design can be traced back to the judgment that produced it.

The scenario selector swaps in Priya's meal-prep subscription, which runs the same three decisions and ends with a single pre-paid meal delivered to one household this week. The Yes and No answers switch positions from one diamond to the next, so read the reasoning on both before you choose.

On a phone-width screen the tree becomes a compact vertical trail of rows above the question card.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the idea in the How to Judge panel and the question on the card.
  2. Click the answer below the drawing area whose reasoning holds for the founder's idea.
  3. If the feedback turns amber, read why the judgment doesn't hold, then choose again.
  4. When a judgment holds, read the design note it adds to the tree, then judge the next diamond.
  5. After all three diamonds, compare the combined design on the card with the three design notes in the tree.
  6. Use the scenario selector to switch between Jordan's grooming van and Priya's meal-prep subscription. Click Reset to return to the first diamond.

The status line next to the selector shows which decision you are on and how many times you have had to reconsider since the last reset.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Given a venture scenario, learners evaluate which lean-test principles (service before product, manual before automated, pre-selling before building) apply, and justify a resulting minimum testable iteration design.

Bloom Level: Evaluate (L5). Bloom Verb: justify.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 6 reading on the minimum viable offer
  • Chapter 10 reading through "Three Rules for a Lean Test"

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Solo run on Jordan (4 min): Each participant works through Jordan's three diamonds and notes how many times they had to reconsider.
  2. Name the objection (4 min): As a group, look at each No answer ("the van comes first," "appointments will get lost without an app," "it isn't fair to ask for money yet"). Discuss why each sounds responsible and why it still delays the one question that matters: will a real customer pay for this now?
  3. Priya in pairs (3 min): Pairs switch to Priya's scenario. Before clicking, each partner predicts her final design in one sentence, then compares it with the card.
  4. Your own venture (4 min): Each participant answers the three questions for their own idea, writes one design note per principle, and combines them into a one-sentence minimum testable iteration. A partner challenges any part that still needs something built, bought or automated first.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant explain why "the van has to come first" does not hold as a reason to skip a service-first test?
  • Given a new venture, can the participant write a three-part minimum testable iteration and justify each part with the principle behind it?
  • Can the participant explain why a deposit is stronger evidence than a free trial or a stated interest?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Lean startup - Wikipedia - The build-measure-learn approach that lean validation and the minimum testable iteration come from.
  2. Minimum viable product - Wikipedia - The smallest version of a product that can test a hypothesis, including concierge and manual variants that deliver the service by hand.
  3. Pre-order - Wikipedia - Taking orders, and often payment, before an item is available, the mechanism behind pre-selling before building.
  4. Customer development - Wikipedia - Steve Blank's method of testing business hypotheses with real customers before scaling.
  5. The Lean Startup by Eric Ries (2011) - The book that popularized the minimum viable product and the practice of testing an idea with the smallest possible experiment.

docs.title: Minimum Viable Offer Slider
docs.text: Run the Minimum Viable Offer Slider MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Jordan's full imagined mobile dog-grooming business has eight features. A minimum viable offer keeps only the ones the offer cannot work without. This MicroSim puts all eight on one checklist and sets the offer's scope with a single slider, from 0 (the bare minimum) to 100 (the full imagined business).

Each feature has a scope threshold. When the slider is at or above a feature's threshold, the feature is checked and in the offer. Below it, the feature fades to gray.

Feature Joins the offer at scope Basic wash and brush-out 0 (core) At the customer's home 0 (core) Text-message booking 10 Nail trim add-on 30 Multiple dog breeds/sizes supported 40 Online booking calendar 55 Flea/tick treatment option 65 Branded van and uniform 85

Two features never leave: the wash and brush-out, and the visit to the customer's home. Take either one away and there is no mobile grooming offer left to test, so they are the essential core. The other six are removable add-ons.

The panel names the tier the current scope falls in:

  • Minimum Viable Offer (0-25): just enough to test the core problem
  • Initial Offer (26-50): still testable, but every add-on is one more assumption
  • Established Offering (51-100): the full imagined business, not a first test

A three-zone meter marks where the scope sits. On wider screens the panel also states Jordan's offer in one sentence, with a word count. The sentence grows from 8 words at the core to 32 words at full scope, so you can see each feature cost the offer some clarity.

The slider starts at 15: a wash and brush-out at the customer's home, booked by text. That is Jordan's actual initial offer from the chapter.

On a phone-width screen the panel stacks above the checklist and the one-sentence offer is hidden.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the checklist at the starting scope of 15. The three checked features are Jordan's actual initial offer.
  2. Click Reset to 0. Only the two core features remain. Decide whether either one could be cut.
  3. Drag the Offer Scope slider to the right. Watch each add-on join the offer at its threshold, and note where the tier changes at 26 and 51.
  4. On a wide screen, compare the one-sentence offer at 15 with the one at 100.
  5. After you click the slider, the left and right arrow keys move it one step at a time.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will apply the concept of a minimum viable offer to Jordan's draft business idea by adjusting the offer's scope and identifying which features are essential to the core offering and which are removable.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3). Bloom Verb: apply.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 5: Defining the Real Problem
  • Chapter 6 reading through "Keeping the First Offer Small"

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Find the core (3 min): The facilitator shares the screen and clicks Reset to 0. Participants type in the chat why neither remaining feature can be removed without breaking the offer.
  2. Defend or cut (5 min): In breakout pairs, one partner picks an add-on and argues it belongs in Jordan's first offer. The other asks, "Would the first customer miss it?" Pairs agree on a scope value and report it back with the matching one-sentence offer.
  3. Slide your own offer (5 min): Each participant lists six to eight features of their own draft business idea, gives each one a scope threshold from 0 to 100, and marks the features at threshold 0. They then write their minimum viable offer in one sentence of 15 words or fewer.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant name Jordan's two core features and explain why each is essential?
  • Given a scope value such as 45, can the participant predict which features are in the offer and which tier it falls in before moving the slider?
  • Can the participant explain why a branded van belongs in an established offering but not in a first test?
  • Does the participant's own minimum viable offer contain only features the offer cannot work without?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Minimum viable product - Wikipedia - The smallest version of a product that can test a business hypothesis with real customers, the product-development idea behind a minimum viable offer.
  2. Lean startup - Wikipedia - The build-measure-learn loop that treats each offer as an experiment to be tested and refined.
  3. Scope creep - Wikipedia - How a project's scope grows one reasonable-sounding addition at a time, the pressure this slider makes visible.
  4. MoSCoW method - Wikipedia - A prioritization technique that sorts features into must have, should have, could have, and won't have, a close cousin of core versus add-on.
  5. The Lean Startup by Eric Ries (2011) - The book that popularized the minimum viable product and validated learning for early-stage founders.

docs.title: One-Sentence Value Proposition Builder
docs.text: Run the One-Sentence Value Proposition Builder MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Jordan's finished value proposition follows a pattern with four parts:

[Target Customer] gets [Core Benefit], from [Founder Advantage], unlike [Main Alternative].

Each part answers one question a stranger would ask:

Part Question it answers Jordan's wording Priya's wording Target Customer Who is it for? busy dog owners without easy groomer access dual-income parents on rotating shifts Core Benefit What do they get? grooming without losing an afternoon a real dinner without any advance planning Founder Advantage Why you? someone they already trust in the neighborhood someone who understands unpredictable schedules firsthand Main Alternative Compared with what? the booked-solid groomer across town another night of takeout

This MicroSim has one dropdown for each part. Every dropdown offers Jordan's wording, Priya's wording, and Write your own, which opens a text box beside the dropdown. The preview card rebuilds the sentence on every change, as you type, and wraps it to fit the screen. Each part keeps its own color, and a missing part stays as a bracketed placeholder. The verb agrees with the customer: "parents get" but "a nurse gets".

Below the preview, the sentence gets formative feedback:

  • Parts filled in: a counter shows how many of the four parts are done.
  • Read time: once all four parts are in, a word count and an estimated read time at about 4 words per second. Green means 8 seconds or less, amber means 9-10 seconds, and dark orange means over the ten-second goal from the chapter.
  • One message: the most important next step. In priority order, the message flags a missing part, parts mixed from two founders, generic words that any competitor could claim (such as "affordable" or "high quality"), and a sentence that is too long to read in ten seconds. A complete sentence gets a next step instead.

Both founders' versions come in at about 7 seconds (27 and 25 words).

On a phone-width screen each role label moves above its dropdown and the button labels shorten.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click Load Jordan's Version and read the finished sentence. Match each colored part to its dropdown.
  2. Click Load Priya's Version and compare. The template is the same; every part changes.
  3. Change one dropdown back to Jordan's wording. Read the warning about mixing two ventures.
  4. Click Clear, then choose Write your own in each dropdown and type the four parts for your own idea. Watch the sentence, word count, and read time update as you type.
  5. Revise until the message box turns green, then copy your sentence out for the five-second test.

docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will compose a one-sentence value proposition for their own venture by choosing or writing a target customer, core benefit, founder advantage, and main alternative, and revise it until it reads clearly in under ten seconds.

Bloom Level: Create (L6). Bloom Verb: compose.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15-20 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 8: Value Proposition: Benefit & Advantage (the value statement)
  • Chapter 12 reading through "The One-Sentence Value Proposition"

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Take apart a finished example (3 min): The facilitator shares the screen and loads Jordan's version. Participants name which question each colored part answers.
  2. Break it on purpose (2 min): The facilitator swaps one part to Priya's wording. The group explains in the chat why the mixed sentence no longer describes one business.
  3. Compose your own (7 min): Each participant chooses Write your own in all four dropdowns and types the parts for their own venture, revising until the message box turns green and the read time is under ten seconds.
  4. Five-second swap (5 min): In breakout pairs, each partner shows their sentence for five seconds, hides it, and asks the other to say back what the business offers. Partners then cut any word the listener didn't need.

  • Is the sentence 32 words or fewer, so it reads in about 8 seconds or less?

  • Can the participant explain why a sentence mixing two ventures' parts fails even though it is grammatical?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Value proposition - Wikipedia - The promise of value a business makes to a specific customer, the idea this sentence compresses.
  2. Unique selling proposition - Wikipedia - The single most compelling point of difference, which the Founder Advantage and Main Alternative parts make explicit.
  3. Elevator pitch - Wikipedia - The short spoken form of a value proposition that grows out of the one-sentence version.
  4. Words per minute - Wikipedia - Typical adult reading speeds, the basis for the read-time estimate of about 4 words per second.
  5. Value Proposition Design by Alexander Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur, Greg Bernarda, and Alan Smith (2014) - A practical guide to matching a product's value to a specific customer's jobs, pains, and gains.

docs.title: Persevere vs Pivot Signal Checker
docs.text: Run the Persevere vs Pivot Signal Checker MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
After a lean test, the founder has to decide what the result means. This MicroSim breaks that call into three evidence signals, one for each of the first three canvas elements:

  • Problem Validated? Target customers raise the pain without being prompted and rank it a priority.
  • Solution Got Payment Signals? Money changed hands, even a small deposit. Likes and "sounds great!" don't count.
  • Customer Definition Confirmed? The people who felt the pain or paid match the target customer you defined.

Check a signal only when its evidence clears the bar. The verdict panel updates the moment a signal changes. The panel's color shows the kind of verdict: green for persevere, fox orange for a pivot, gray for a kill. The panel also gives a one-sentence justification. A row of chips shows what happens to each element: Keep the elements that have evidence, Change the element the pivot names, and Retest anything else.

Problem Solution Customer Verdict on on on Persevere on off on Pivot the Solution (Priya's scenario) on on off Pivot the Customer (revisit Chapter 4) on off off Pivot the Customer (revisit Chapter 4) off any any Pivot the Problem (revisit Chapter 5) off off off Kill Decision (see Chapter 10)

All three signals off is a kill, not a problem pivot: nothing has evidence behind it, so there is nothing to keep. The chapter's rules don't name the problem-only pattern. Here it counts as a customer pivot, because the founder has to confirm who feels the pain before testing a new offer on anyone.

Load Priya's Evidence is a worked example. It sets Priya's signals and notes, line by line, whether each piece of her evidence clears its bar. Her problem and customer are validated, but only 1 of 10 families said yes to her advance-planning subscription. That pattern points to Pivot the Solution.

Try a Scenario gives you four practice ventures to judge on your own. Each card lists one line of evidence per signal. Some lines are traps: a post with 15 likes and no deposits, or a pain that only came up after a leading question. After you click Check My Reading, each signal turns green (read honestly) or amber (misread) with the reason. The panel then shows the verdict the evidence actually supports.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start in Explore mode: check and uncheck the three signals and watch the verdict change.
  2. Click Load Priya's Evidence to walk through a worked example. Try unchecking a signal to see how the verdict would change, then click Check My Reading to compare with her honest reading.
  3. Click Try a Scenario. Read each line of evidence against the bar printed above it.
  4. Check only the signals whose evidence clears the bar. The panel shows the verdict your reading points to.
  5. Click Check My Reading for feedback on each signal and the verdict the evidence supports. Then click Next Scenario.
  6. After the fourth scenario, the card shows how many you read honestly on the first try. Click Try Again for the same four ventures in a new order.
  7. Click Reset at any time to return to Explore mode with every signal off.

On wide screens the evidence card and the verdict panel sit side by side. On a phone the panel moves below the card, and after a check the card may shorten each evidence line to its feedback note so everything fits.
